nodes.label: Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach, 9th ed., Chapter 2 Application Layer
nodes.author: J.F. Kurose and K.W. Ross
nodes.norm_label: computer networking: a top-down approach, 9th ed., chapter 2 application layer
nodes.rationale: Pearson 2025 slides covering application-layer principles, HTTP, e-mail, DNS, video/CDNs, and socket programming. Copyright 1996-2025.

nodes.label: Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach, Chapter 1
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.norm_label: computer networking: a top-down approach, chapter 1
nodes.rationale: Chapter goal is a big-picture vocabulary of the Internet, protocols, edge and core, performance, layering, security, and history, with depth deferred to later chapters.

nodes.label: AS-PATH
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: BGP route attribute listing the ASes through which a prefix advertisement has passed. Shortest AS-PATH is the second BGP route-selection criterion, after local preference.

nodes.label: Autonomous System
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Routers are aggregated into regions (autonomous systems, or domains) because a flat Internet cannot store every destination or flood every route, and each network administration wants to control routing inside its own network.

nodes.label: Bellman-Ford Equation
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Dynamic-programming basis of distance-vector routing: Dx(y) = min over neighbors v of cx,v + Dv(y). The neighbor achieving the minimum is the next hop.

nodes.label: BGP
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Border Gateway Protocol, the de facto inter-domain routing protocol and the glue that holds the Internet together. It is a path-vector protocol: peers advertise prefix reachability over a semi-permanent TCP session. Import and export policy decide which paths are accepted and advertised. A typical policy is that an ISP carries traffic to and from its customers and does not provide transit between other ISPs.

nodes.label: BGP Messages
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Peers exchange OPEN (open the TCP session and authenticate), UPDATE (advertise or withdraw a path), KEEPALIVE (hold the session and ACK OPEN), and NOTIFICATION (report errors and close the connection).

nodes.label: BGP Route Selection
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: When more than one route to a destination is known, select in order: local preference (policy), shortest AS-PATH, closest NEXT-HOP (hot potato), then additional criteria.

nodes.label: Count-to-Infinity Problem
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Bad news travels slowly in distance-vector routing. After a link-cost increase, neighbors repeatedly adopt each other's stale path and increment the cost one hop at a time, forming a routing loop. Good news (a cost decrease) converges quickly.

nodes.label: Dijkstra's Algorithm
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Iterative least-cost algorithm from one source. After k iterations the least-cost path to k destinations is known. Complexity is O(n^2), with O(n log n) implementations possible; link-state dissemination is also O(n^2). Oscillations are possible when link costs depend on traffic volume. Ties may be broken arbitrarily.

nodes.label: Distance-Vector Routing
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Decentralized, iterative, and asynchronous: each router starts knowing only neighbor link costs, exchanges distance-vector estimates with neighbors, and notifies neighbors only when its vector changes. Errors, including a false low-cost path, can black-hole traffic and propagate.

nodes.label: eBGP
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: External BGP sessions between gateway routers in neighboring ASes, used to obtain destination-prefix reachability and to advertise reachability onward.

nodes.label: EIGRP
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol, a distance-vector intra-AS protocol. It was Cisco-proprietary for decades and became open in 2013.

nodes.label: Forwarding
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Data-plane function that moves a packet from a router's input to the appropriate output using values in the arriving packet header.

nodes.label: Gateway Router
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Router at the edge of its AS with links to routers in other ASes. It runs inter-domain routing as well as intra-domain routing, and learns which external destinations are reachable through which neighboring AS.

nodes.label: Google ORION
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Google's SDN control plane (NSDI 2021) for the Jupiter datacenter network and the B4 WAN. Intradomain routing, iBGP, and traffic engineering run as applications on the ORION core. Edge-to-edge flow controls such as CoFlow scheduling meet contract SLAs. The core uses pub-sub distributed microservices, and OpenFlow is used for switch signaling and monitoring. ORION provides intradomain services inside Google's network. Amin Vahdat's argument is that configuring a logical network in one controller is simpler than letting every element learn its role from neighbors.

nodes.label: Hierarchical OSPF
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Two-level hierarchy of local areas and a backbone. Link-state advertisements are flooded only inside an area or the backbone, so a router has detailed topology only for its area. Area border routers summarize distances; backbone routers run OSPF on the backbone; boundary routers connect to other ASes.

nodes.label: Hot Potato Routing
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: When several local gateways can reach a prefix, choose the gateway with the least intra-domain cost and ignore inter-domain cost, even if that path has more AS hops.

nodes.label: iBGP
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Internal BGP sessions that propagate reachability learned from neighboring ASes to all routers inside the AS. Gateway routers run both eBGP and iBGP.

nodes.label: ICMP
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Internet Control Message Protocol, used by hosts and routers for network-level information. Messages are carried in IP datagrams and contain a type, a code, and the first 8 bytes of the datagram that caused the error. Uses include error reporting (unreachable network, host, protocol, or port) and echo request/reply used by ping. Type 11 code 0 is TTL expired; type 3 code 3 is port unreachable. Source quench (type 4 code 0) is unused.

nodes.label: Inter-AS Routing
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Routing among ASes. Policy dominates performance: an administration wants control over how its traffic is routed and who routes through its network. Hierarchy also reduces table size and update traffic.

nodes.label: Intra-AS Routing
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Routing among routers inside one AS. All routers in an AS run the same intra-domain protocol; different ASes may run different ones. A single administrator makes policy less important than performance.

nodes.label: IS-IS
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: ISO link-state intra-AS protocol, not an RFC standard, described as essentially the same as OSPF.

nodes.label: Link-State Routing
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Global algorithm: every router has the complete topology and link costs, obtained by link-state broadcast, and computes its own forwarding table. A router can advertise an incorrect link cost, but each router computes only its own table.

nodes.label: Local Preference
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: BGP route attribute used first in route selection. It encodes a policy decision and outranks shortest AS-PATH and hot-potato next hop.

nodes.label: MIB
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Management Information Base: a device's operational and some configuration data, organized as a MIB module. About 400 MIB modules are defined in RFCs, plus many vendor-specific modules. UDP examples include UDPInDatagrams and udpTable, identified by object IDs under 1.3.6.1.2.1.7.

nodes.label: NETCONF
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Network-wide configuration protocol between a managing server and managed devices. It retrieves, sets, modifies, and activates configuration, supports atomic commit across devices, queries operational data, and subscribes to notifications. Messages are XML RPCs over a secure transport such as TLS. Operations include get-config, get, edit-config, lock, unlock, create-subscription, and notification. A session starts with hello and ends with close-session.

nodes.label: Network Management
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Deployment, integration, and coordination of hardware, software, and people to monitor, test, poll, configure, analyze, evaluate, and control network resources so real-time performance and QoS are met at reasonable cost. Components are a managing server, managed devices with agents, device data, and a management protocol. Operator approaches include CLI, SNMP/MIB, and NETCONF/YANG.

nodes.label: NEXT-HOP
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: BGP route attribute identifying the specific internal-AS router that is the next hop toward the next AS. Closest NEXT-HOP is the third route-selection criterion.

nodes.label: Northbound API
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Interface by which the SDN controller exposes abstractions to network-control applications above it. Examples include a RESTful API and an intent interface.

nodes.label: ODL
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Named with ONOS as a practical SDN controller implementation. The slides list it in the chapter goals and summary and do not describe its internals.

nodes.label: ONOS
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Early influential open-source SDN controller. Control apps are separate from the controller. An intent framework specifies a service as what rather than how. A distributed core emphasizes reliability, replication, and scaling. Southbound protocols include OpenFlow, NETCONF, and OVSDB; northbound abstractions include REST and intent.

nodes.label: OpenFlow
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Protocol between an SDN controller and a switch, carried over TCP with optional encryption. Message classes are controller-to-switch, asynchronous switch-to-controller, and symmetric. Distinct from the OpenFlow API, which specifies generalized forwarding actions. Controller-to-switch messages include features, configure, modify-state, and packet-out; switch-to-controller messages include packet-in, flow-removed, and port status.

nodes.label: OSPF
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Open Shortest Path First: a publicly available link-state intra-AS protocol. Each router floods link-state advertisements directly over IP, not TCP or UDP, may use bandwidth or delay as link cost, and runs Dijkstra. All OSPF messages are authenticated to prevent malicious intrusion.

nodes.label: Per-Router Control Plane
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Traditional structure in which a routing-algorithm component in every router interacts with other routers to compute that router's forwarding table.

nodes.label: RIP
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Routing Information Protocol, a classic distance-vector intra-AS protocol that exchanges distance vectors every 30 seconds. No longer widely used.

nodes.label: Routing
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Control-plane function that determines the route packets take from source to destination, seeking a good path such as least cost, fastest, or least congested.

nodes.label: SDN Control Plane
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Logically centralized control: a remote controller computes and installs forwarding tables. Motivated by easier management, flexible traffic flows, centralized programming of tables, and an open non-proprietary control plane.

nodes.label: SDN Controller
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Network operating system that maintains network state, talks to control applications above and to switches below, and is implemented as a distributed system for performance, scalability, fault tolerance, and robustness. Its layers are device communication, network-wide state management, and an interface for control apps.

nodes.label: SMI
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Structure of Management Information, the data-definition language for SNMP MIB variables.

nodes.label: SNMP
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Simple Network Management Protocol. A managing server queries and sets device data in a MIB. Modes are request/response and trap. Message types are GetRequest, GetNextRequest, GetBulkRequest, SetRequest, Response, and Trap.

nodes.label: Southbound API
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Interface by which the SDN controller communicates with network switches below it. It defines what in the switch is controllable.

nodes.label: Traceroute
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Source sends UDP probes with increasing TTL. Each router that expires the TTL returns ICMP type 11 code 0, and the source records RTTs. The destination returns ICMP port unreachable (type 3 code 3), which stops the trace.

nodes.label: YANG
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Data-modeling language for the structure, syntax, and semantics of NETCONF management data. It has built-in types like SMI, can generate XML describing a device, and can express constraints that a valid configuration must satisfy.

nodes.label: Network Layer Control Plane
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: Chapter 5 of Kurose and Ross, Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach, 9th edition (Pearson, 2025), covers routing algorithms, OSPF, BGP, SDN controllers, ICMP, and SNMP/NETCONF/YANG.

nodes.label: Traffic Engineering
nodes.author: Jim Kurose, Keith Ross
nodes.rationale: With destination-based link-state and distance-vector routing, link weights are the only control knobs. An operator cannot force a specific path, split traffic across two paths, or treat two traffic classes differently without a new algorithm. Generalized forwarding and SDN can realize any desired routing.

nodes.label: Access Network
nodes.rationale: Connects end systems to an edge router. Residential access uses cable or DSL; institutional access mixes Ethernet and WiFi; mobile access uses WiFi and 4G/5G. A home network often combines a cable or DSL modem with a router, firewall, and NAT, plus wired Ethernet and a WiFi access point.

nodes.label: Application Layer
nodes.rationale: Supports network applications. Named protocols include HTTP, IMAP, SMTP, and DNS. Applications exchange messages using the transport layer's service. OSI presentation and session services, if needed, are implemented here because the Internet stack has no separate layers for them.

nodes.label: ARPAnet
nodes.rationale: Conceived in 1967 by the Advanced Research Projects Agency; first node operational in 1969. By 1972 it had a public demo, the first host-to-host protocol NCP, the first email program, and 15 nodes. It had 200 nodes by 1979 and was decommissioned in the early 1990s. Kleinrock's 1961 queueing theory and Baran's 1964 military packet-switching work are cited as the early justification for packet switching.

nodes.label: Content Provider Network
nodes.rationale: Providers such as Google, Microsoft, Akamai, and Facebook run private networks that connect their data centers to the Internet, often bypassing tier-1 and regional ISPs, so content is close to end users.

nodes.label: DNS
nodes.rationale: Application-layer protocol defined in 1983 for name-to-IP-address translation.

nodes.label: Digital Subscriber Line (DSL)
nodes.rationale: Uses the existing telephone line to a central-office DSLAM. Voice and data travel at different frequencies on a dedicated line, so the access line is not shared among homes the way cable is. Cited rates are 24-52 Mbps downstream and 3.5-16 Mbps upstream. Data goes to the Internet and voice to the telephone network.

nodes.label: Ethernet
nodes.rationale: Wired link technology: enterprise access at 100 Mbps, 1 Gbps, and 10 Gbps, and twisted-pair categories cited for 100 Mbps through 10 Gbps Ethernet. Developed at Xerox PARC in 1976. Shared Ethernet is a broadcast medium that enables packet sniffing.

nodes.label: Firewall
nodes.rationale: Specialized middlebox in access and core networks. Off-by-default filtering of incoming packets restricts senders, receivers, and applications, and is also a place to detect or react to denial-of-service attacks. Home access devices often combine the router, firewall, and NAT.

nodes.label: Hybrid Fiber Coax (HFC)
nodes.rationale: Cable access sends data and TV at different frequencies over a shared cable distribution network. Asymmetric: about 40 Mbps to 1.2 Gbps downstream and 30-100 Mbps upstream. Homes share the path to the cable headend and CMTS, which attaches to the ISP.

nodes.label: Host (End System)
nodes.rationale: Hosts are end systems running network applications at the Internet edge, acting as clients and servers. Servers often sit in data centers. A sending host breaks an application message into packets of L bits and transmits them into the access network at link rate R.

nodes.label: HTTP
nodes.rationale: Application protocol for the Web. The running example is a GET of http://gaia.cs.umass.edu/kurose_ross after a TCP connection handshake. History credits HTML and HTTP to Berners-Lee.

nodes.label: Internet
nodes.rationale: Nuts-and-bolts view: a network of networks of hosts, packet switches, and links managed by organizations. Services view: infrastructure for networked applications plus a programming interface, analogous to the postal service, that lets distributed apps send and receive using a transport service.

nodes.label: IP
nodes.rationale: Network-layer protocol that carries datagrams from source host to destination host. DNS maps names to IP addresses.

nodes.label: Internet Service Provider (ISP)
nodes.rationale: Hosts connect through access ISPs, which must be interconnected so any two hosts can exchange packets. A full mesh of access ISPs is O(N^2) and does not scale. One global transit ISP works commercially, then competitors appear, then peering, regional ISPs, and content-provider networks. Evolution is driven by economics and national policy. Customer and provider ISPs have an economic agreement.

nodes.label: Internet Exchange Point (IXP)
nodes.rationale: Competing global ISPs interconnect at Internet exchange points over peering links rather than only through a single transit provider.

nodes.label: Link Layer
nodes.rationale: Transfers data between neighboring network elements. Named technologies: Ethernet, 802.11 WiFi, and PPP. Encapsulates the datagram with header Hl to form a frame and moves that frame to the next host using the physical layer.

nodes.label: Network Core
nodes.rationale: Mesh of interconnected routers that forwards packets hop by hop from source to destination. Two key functions are forwarding (local) and routing (global).

nodes.label: Network Edge
nodes.rationale: The edge is hosts (clients and servers, servers often in data centers) plus the access networks and physical media that connect them to the core.

nodes.label: Network Layer
nodes.rationale: Routes datagrams from source to destination using IP and routing protocols. Encapsulates the transport segment with header Hn and transfers it host-to-host using link-layer services.

nodes.label: Packet Switch
nodes.rationale: Routers and switches forward packets. In the end-to-end encapsulation picture a router handles headers through the network layer, while a switch handles link and physical headers.

nodes.label: Physical Layer
nodes.rationale: Moves bits on the wire between a transmitter and a receiver.

nodes.label: Physical Media
nodes.rationale: Guided media (twisted pair, coax, fiber) carry signals in a solid; unguided radio propagates freely and is affected by reflection, obstruction, and interference. Fiber offers tens to hundreds of Gbps and low error rates because it is immune to electromagnetic noise. Radio types include WiFi, 4G/5G, Bluetooth, terrestrial microwave, and satellite (geostationary delay about 270 ms; Starlink cited for downlink).

nodes.label: Protocol
nodes.rationale: Protocols define the format and order of messages sent and received among network entities and the actions taken on transmission, receipt, or other events. All Internet communication is governed by protocols.

nodes.label: Software-Defined Networking (SDN)
nodes.rationale: Dated to 2008 in the era of broadband access, 4G/5G and WiFi, provider-owned networks, cloud (Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure), and smartphones. The chapter names SDN without defining its mechanism.

nodes.label: TCP
nodes.rationale: Transport protocol providing process-to-process transfer. The protocol walk-through shows a TCP connection request and response before the application exchange. TCP congestion control was added in 1988 because packet switching can congest.

nodes.label: TCP/IP
nodes.rationale: Deployed in 1983 during the proliferation of networks (CSnet, BITnet, NSFnet, Minitel), alongside SMTP (1982), DNS (1983), FTP (1985), and TCP congestion control (1988).

nodes.label: Tier-1 ISP
nodes.rationale: A small number of well-connected commercial ISPs (examples: Level 3, Sprint, AT&T, NTT) with national and international coverage sit at the center of the Internet.

nodes.label: Traceroute
nodes.rationale: Measures delay from a source to each router along the path toward a destination. For hop i it sends three probes whose time-to-live is i; router i returns the packets and the sender records the interval. A star means no response. The chapter's example is gaia.cs.umass.edu to www.eurecom.fr, including a trans-oceanic link.

nodes.label: Transport Layer
nodes.rationale: Process-to-process data transfer, exemplified by TCP and UDP. Encapsulates the application message M with header Ht to form a segment, and transfers that message using the network layer, reliably in the TCP case.

nodes.label: WiFi (IEEE 802.11)
nodes.rationale: Wireless LAN within or around a building. End systems reach a router via a base station (access point). Cited rates include 11, 54, and 450 Mbps for 802.11b/g/n. Shared wireless media can be sniffed.

nodes.label: Cerf and Kahn Internetworking Principles
nodes.rationale: 1974 architecture for interconnecting networks, stated as what defines today's Internet: minimalism and autonomy so networks interconnect with no internal changes, a best-effort service model, stateless routing, and decentralized control.

nodes.label: Circuit Switching
nodes.rationale: End-to-end resources are reserved for a call, giving guaranteed circuit-like performance, but an idle circuit is not shared. Common in traditional telephone networks. Implemented by FDM or TDM. On the example 1 Gb/s link, circuit switching supports 10 users who each need 100 Mb/s.

nodes.label: Denial of Service (DoS)
nodes.rationale: Attackers make a server or bandwidth unavailable to legitimate traffic by overwhelming it with bogus traffic. The chapter's sketch is: select a target, compromise hosts around the network (a botnet), and send packets to the target from those hosts.

nodes.label: Encapsulation
nodes.rationale: Each layer wraps the unit from above with its own header so it can implement its service: application message M, transport segment Ht+M, network datagram Hn+segment, link frame Hl+datagram. At each hop, routers and switches use and strip or add the headers for the layers they implement.

nodes.label: Frequency Division Multiplexing (FDM)
nodes.rationale: Divides a link into frequency bands so each call transmits continuously at the rate of its narrow band. Cable access also uses FDM so video and data occupy different channels on a shared coax plant.

nodes.label: Forwarding
nodes.rationale: Also called switching. Local action: move an arriving packet from the router's input link to the output link selected by a local forwarding table indexed by the destination address in the packet header.

nodes.label: Internet Protocol Stack
nodes.rationale: Layering organizes a complex system: each layer implements a service by its own actions while relying on the layer below. Explicit structure makes the pieces and their relationships discussable, and modularization lets one layer's implementation change transparently to the rest of the system. The Internet stack has five layers: application, transport, network, link, and physical.

nodes.label: IP Spoofing
nodes.rationale: Injection of a packet with a false source address so the sender claims another host's identity.

nodes.label: Network Security
nodes.rationale: The Internet was not originally designed with much security; the original vision was mutually trusting users on a transparent network, so designers later played catch-up and put security considerations in all layers. Defenses named here: authentication (a SIM gives hardware identity in cellular networks; the traditional Internet has no such assist), confidentiality via encryption, integrity via digital signatures, password-protected VPNs, and firewalls. Deeper treatment is deferred to Chapter 8.

nodes.label: Nodal Delay
nodes.rationale: Total nodal delay is dnodal = dproc + dqueue + dtrans + dprop. Transmission delay and propagation delay are different quantities; the caravan analogy separates time to push the packet onto the link from time for bits to travel to the next node.

nodes.label: ISO/OSI Reference Model
nodes.rationale: Seven-layer model. Presentation (encryption, compression, machine-specific data meaning) and session (synchronization, checkpointing, recovery of data exchange) are absent from the Internet stack. If those services are needed they must be implemented in the application.

nodes.label: Packet Loss
nodes.rationale: Router buffers are finite. If the arrival rate to a link exceeds its transmission rate long enough for the buffer to fill, arriving packets are dropped. A lost packet may be retransmitted by the previous node, by the source end system, or not at all.

nodes.label: Packet Sniffing
nodes.rationale: On broadcast media (shared Ethernet, wireless), a promiscuous interface can read and record every packet that passes, including passwords. Wireshark is the packet sniffer used in the end-of-chapter labs; the closing slide shows it capturing a copy of Ethernet frames.

nodes.label: Packet Switching
nodes.rationale: Hosts break application messages into packets that routers forward. Suited to bursty data because of statistical resource sharing and no call setup. A 1 Gb/s link with users active 10% of the time at 100 Mb/s can admit far more than the 10 circuit-switched users; with 35 users the chance more than 10 are active is under 0.0004. Congestion can cause delay and loss, so reliable transfer and congestion control are needed. Making packet switching behave like circuits is described as complicated.

nodes.label: Processing Delay
nodes.rationale: Time to check bit errors and choose the output link. Typically under a microsecond.

nodes.label: Propagation Delay
nodes.rationale: Time for a bit to travel a physical link of length d at propagation speed s (about 2×10^8 m/s): dprop = d/s. Distinct from transmission delay.

nodes.label: Queueing Delay
nodes.rationale: Time waiting at an output link when packets arrive faster than the link can send them. Depends on congestion. Traffic intensity La/R near 0 means small average delay, near 1 means large delay, and above 1 means more work arrives than can be served so average delay is infinite.

nodes.label: Routing
nodes.rationale: Global action: routing algorithms determine the source-destination paths packets take. Cerf and Kahn's architecture uses stateless routing and decentralized control.

nodes.label: Store-and-Forward
nodes.rationale: The entire packet must arrive at a router before it can be transmitted on the next link. Pushing an L-bit packet onto a link of rate R takes L/R seconds. Example: L = 10 Kbits and R = 100 Mbps gives a one-hop transmission delay of 0.1 ms.

nodes.label: TCP Congestion Control
nodes.rationale: Packet switching can suffer excessive congestion, delay, and loss, so protocols for reliable data transfer and congestion control are required. TCP congestion control is dated to 1988.

nodes.label: Time Division Multiplexing (TDM)
nodes.rationale: Divides time into slots. Each call gets periodic slots and may transmit at the full wider-band rate only during its slot.

nodes.label: Throughput
nodes.rationale: Rate at which bits are delivered from sender to receiver, instantaneous or average. Average end-end throughput is limited by the bottleneck link. With server link Rs, client link Rc, and n connections sharing a backbone of rate R, per-connection throughput is min(Rc, Rs, R/n). In practice Rc or Rs is often the bottleneck.

nodes.label: Transmission Delay
nodes.rationale: Time to push an L-bit packet onto a link of transmission rate R: dtrans = L/R. Link transmission rate is also called link capacity or bandwidth.

nodes.label: 5G Core Network
nodes.rationale: One core serves many RANs. It is an all-IP core whose services differ from ordinary Internet applications, and most of its specified functions are control-plane services.

nodes.label: 5G New Radio
nodes.rationale: 5G NR keeps OFDMA but allows 15, 30, 60, or 120 kHz subcarriers and up to 100 MHz carrier bandwidth. Low, mid, and high (mmWave) bands trade range for rate.

nodes.label: Ad Hoc Network
nodes.rationale: A wireless network with no infrastructure such as an access point or base station; devices must organize the network themselves.

nodes.label: Access and Mobility Management Function
nodes.rationale: AMF handles connection and reachability, mobility, access authorization, and location services, and is the key function when a device registers.

nodes.label: Base Station
nodes.rationale: Typically wired to the infrastructure and relays packets between the wired network and wireless hosts in its area, such as a 4G/5G cell tower or an 802.11 access point.

nodes.label: Bluetooth Low Energy
nodes.rationale: BLE uses 2 MHz channels (40 total: 3 advertising and 37 data) and, unlike Classic Bluetooth, adds managed flooding. It has a separate controller from Classic Bluetooth.

nodes.label: Bluetooth
nodes.rationale: An ad hoc cable-replacement architecture with its own stack, not the Internet stack. Classic Bluetooth has no network or transport layer and no routing.

nodes.label: Channel Quality Indicator
nodes.rationale: The UE measures reference signals and reports a 4-bit CQI that maps to the modulation, such as which QAM, and the expected throughput the scheduler should assume.

nodes.label: CSMA/CA
nodes.rationale: 802.11 sends the whole frame after the channel is idle for DIFS, with no collision detection. The receiver returns an ACK after SIFS because a hidden terminal may have corrupted the frame, and the backoff doubles after a missing ACK.

nodes.label: Extended Service Set
nodes.rationale: 802.11 treats mobility as a link-layer problem: several basic service sets share one SSID and one layer-3 subnet, with fast re-authentication between them.

nodes.label: Geosynchronous Satellite
nodes.rationale: A GEO satellite is stationary relative to the ground at 35,768 km, covers a wide area, and has about 800 ms RTT.

nodes.label: gNodeB
nodes.rationale: The 5G base station (Next Generation Node B) is the single base station in a RAN and the first-hop relay between user equipment and the mobile core.

nodes.label: GTP-U
nodes.rationale: On the N3 backhaul, the user IP packet is carried inside GTP-U over UDP/IP between the UPF and the base station.

nodes.label: IEEE 802.11
nodes.rationale: The wireless LAN link-layer standard. Frames carry up to four MAC addresses, a duration field for RTS/CTS, and type bits for management, control, and data.

nodes.label: Inter-Satellite Link
nodes.rationale: Links between LEO satellites turn a constellation into a network in the sky, with routing across multiple satellite hops rather than a single bent-pipe hop.

nodes.label: Internet of Things
nodes.rationale: IoT spans meters to kilometers, from hundreds of bits per second for metering up to about 1 Mbps for video, and energy is always a constraint, including devices that run about 10 years without external power.

nodes.label: L2CAP
nodes.rationale: Logical Link Control and Adaptation creates end-to-end channels with reliability, flow control, and segmentation: connection-oriented ACL, connectionless ACL, or synchronous eSCO for audio.

nodes.label: Low Earth Orbit Satellite
nodes.rationale: LEO satellites orbit at 550-1200 km, move about 27,000 km/h, stay in line of sight for 5-15 minutes, and have about 30 ms RTT. Wide coverage needs a constellation and inter-satellite links.

nodes.label: LoRaWAN
nodes.rationale: Named with LTE-M as a low-power wide-area option, distinct from short-range WiFi, BLE, and Zigbee and from traditional 4G/5G cellular.

nodes.label: 4G LTE
nodes.rationale: 4G LTE uses OFDMA with 15 kHz subcarriers and a maximum carrier bandwidth of 20 MHz. Its base station is the eNodeB and its mobility anchor in the older architecture is the MME.

nodes.label: MIMO
nodes.rationale: Multiple-input multiple-output antennas provide spatial diversity (redundant streams for reliability and range) or spatial multiplexing (independent streams), and multi-user MIMO uses beamforming toward separated users.

nodes.label: OFDM
nodes.rationale: Orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing packs overlapping subcarriers so crosstalk cancels at each subcarrier center, avoiding the guard bands of plain FDM.

nodes.label: OFDMA
nodes.rationale: OFDMA assigns time-frequency resource blocks to users. The slides list it for 4G/5G, WiFi 6, Bluetooth, and satellite.

nodes.label: O-RAN
nodes.rationale: O-RAN splits a formerly monolithic base station into a Central Unit, Distributed Unit, and Radio Unit; where each unit runs is an implementation choice.

nodes.label: Packet Data Convergence Protocol
nodes.rationale: PDCP compresses IP headers and provides ciphering and integrity protection on the RAN user-plane path above RLC, MAC, and PHY.

nodes.label: Bluetooth Piconet
nodes.rationale: A piconet is generally under 10 m and has at most eight devices: one central and up to seven peripherals. Peripherals talk only to the central, which polls them for channel access.

nodes.label: Quadrature Amplitude Modulation
nodes.rationale: m-QAM encodes log2(m) bits in amplitude and phase. The slides show 4-QAM, 16-QAM, and 64-QAM constellations used by WiFi, generalizing QPSK.

nodes.label: Resource Block
nodes.rationale: The smallest scheduling unit assigned to one user. In 4G a resource block is 84 symbols (12 subcarriers by 7 symbols); the base station reassigns blocks about every 1 ms.

nodes.label: Radio Resource Control
nodes.rationale: RRC configures coarse policy for the RAN pipeline, including scheduling priority and security. It is the control plane and does not process user-plane packets.

nodes.label: RTS/CTS
nodes.rationale: A short request-to-send reserves the medium; the base station broadcasts clear-to-send with the duration so every station that hears either frame defers. WiFi 6/7 extends this with multiuser RTS before OFDMA.

nodes.label: Software-Defined RAN
nodes.rationale: SD-RAN refactors RRC into a control-plane proxy and a Real-Time Intelligent Controller. Near-real-time xApps such as load balancing, handover, and QoS share a RAN Network Information Base.

nodes.label: Subscriber Identity Module
nodes.rationale: A SIM or vSIM identifies the subscriber and home network to cellular networks worldwide and holds cryptographic key material also known to the home network.

nodes.label: Session Management Function
nodes.rationale: SMF manages each UE session: IP address allocation, UPF selection, QoS control, and the control aspects of user-plane routing.

nodes.label: Starlink
nodes.rationale: The slides (April 2025) describe about 7,239 operational Starlink LEO satellites in shells at 525, 530, and 535 km, with Internet service and planned inter-satellite links.

nodes.label: Unlicensed Spectrum
nodes.rationale: Unlicensed bands are open to anyone who follows power rules. The slides name 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz WiFi and 3.5 GHz CBRS (private 5G), in contrast to licensed cellular spectrum sold by auction.

nodes.label: User Plane Function
nodes.rationale: Each device is assigned a UPF that relays traffic to the Internet and enforces policy, lawful intercept, usage measurement, and QoS. It also tunnels traffic to the base station over N3.

nodes.label: User Equipment
nodes.rationale: The 5G mobile device. All of its packets pass through the base station, and it reports channel quality and sends scheduling requests on the uplink control channel.

nodes.label: WiFi 6
nodes.rationale: 802.11ax (2020) is WiFi 6, with a theoretical 9.5 Gbps on 2.4 and 5 GHz using OFDM, OFDMA, and MIMO. WiFi 7 (802.11be, 2024) adds 6 GHz and 320 MHz channels.

nodes.label: WiFi Access Point
nodes.rationale: The 802.11 base station that bridges wireless hosts to an institutional wired network and the Internet.

nodes.label: Wireless Host
nodes.rationale: A laptop, smartphone, or IoT device that runs applications and may be stationary or mobile; wireless connectivity does not imply mobility.

nodes.label: Zigbee
nodes.rationale: A short-range IoT radio that shares the unlicensed 2.4 GHz ISM band with WiFi, Bluetooth, and many other consumer devices.

nodes.label: Chapter 7 Wireless and Mobile Networks
nodes.rationale: Kurose and Ross 9th edition slides (Pearson, 2025) covering radio, wireless access, the 5G core, mobility, Bluetooth, satellite, and IoT.

nodes.label: Shannon 1948 Paper
nodes.rationale: The slides attribute the channel-capacity result to Shannon's classic 1948 paper, without a full bibliographic citation.

nodes.label: Adaptive Modulation
nodes.rationale: As interference and transmit power change SNR, the sender switches modulation and power to the highest rate that still meets an acceptable bit-error rate and energy cost.

nodes.label: Bent-Pipe Satellite Architecture
nodes.rationale: A bent pipe is a single satellite hop between base stations, so the satellite is a link in the sky rather than a router.

nodes.label: Control and User Plane Separation
nodes.rationale: CUPS splits 5G control-plane functions and services from the user-plane forwarding path, with well-defined interfaces such as N1, N2, N3, and N4 between them.

nodes.label: Discontinuous Reception
nodes.rationale: After an inactivity timer the device enters short DRX, then long DRX. Longer sleep saves energy but adds latency and can affect TCP, and the base station buffers downlink packets until the device wakes.

nodes.label: Bluetooth Frequency Hopping
nodes.rationale: A piconet hops among 79 channels, one frequency per 625 microsecond slot, so an interferer on one ISM channel hits only an occasional slot and the frame is retried on another frequency.

nodes.label: 5G Handover
nodes.rationale: The device changes its point of attachment when the target base station has a stronger signal or less load. The source station forwards data until the SMF points the UPF tunnel at the target.

nodes.label: Hidden Terminal Problem
nodes.rationale: Path loss and obstacles let A hear B and B hear C while A and C cannot hear each other, so they collide at B without knowing it.

nodes.label: Multipath Propagation
nodes.rationale: Reflections off the ground and buildings arrive at slightly different times than the line-of-sight path; coherence time shrinks as frequency and receiver speed rise.

nodes.label: Path Loss
nodes.rationale: Radio power falls with frequency and distance, roughly (fd)^n, with n about 2 in free space, 2.7-3.5 in urban settings, and 3-6 indoors.

nodes.label: Proportional Fairness Scheduling
nodes.rationale: PF picks the user and resource block that maximize expected rate over recent achieved rate, combining maximum-throughput scheduling with blind equal throughput. Standards leave this choice to the operator.

nodes.label: Shannon Capacity
nodes.rationale: C = B log2(1 + SNR) is the maximum rate given bandwidth and SNR. Capacity scales linearly with bandwidth and only logarithmically with high SNR.

nodes.label: Signal-to-Noise Ratio
nodes.rationale: SNR in dB is 10 log10 of received signal power over noise power. The slides cite a cellular lower limit around -10 to -6 dB and a WiFi lower limit around 20 dB.

nodes.label: Connection state machine
nodes.rationale: The client sends INITIAL and moves through CONNECTING. The server caches the HANDSHAKE reply. After the signature is verified and the key is pinned, both sides derive keys with HKDF and become ESTABLISHED. AUTH then yields ONLINE and a PEERS push, or AUTH_FAIL. Idle beyond 20 seconds or CLOSE moves the user OFFLINE and updates PEERS. An unexpected loss enters RECONNECTING with backoff 1, 2, 4, up to 15 seconds and an automatic login.

nodes.label: HANDSHAKE packet 0x02
nodes.rationale: Cleartext server hello: 4-byte server connection id, 32-byte X25519 public key, 32-byte Ed25519 public key, and a 64-byte signature over the transcript.

nodes.label: INITIAL packet 0x01
nodes.rationale: Cleartext client hello: 4-byte client connection id plus a 32-byte X25519 public key. The client resends with backoff from 0.25 s to 1 s.

nodes.label: CollabNet
nodes.rationale: Chat with broadcast and private messages, an online user list, and reliable file transfer, all on raw UDP with a handwritten multi-stream transport and AES-256-GCM. The UI is HTML and JavaScript served by a handwritten HTTP server.

nodes.label: 1200-byte datagram
nodes.rationale: Layout is type (1 byte), destination connection id (4 bytes), packet number (8 bytes), encrypted frames up to 1171 bytes, and a 16-byte GCM tag. The 13-byte header is authenticated as additional data. Datagrams stay at or below 1200 bytes, under the MTU, and payload is cut into STREAM frames. That avoids IP fragmentation, which would drop the whole datagram if one fragment were lost.

nodes.label: Handshake security
nodes.rationale: There is no stock TLS on this UDP transport, so standard primitives are composed. Ephemeral X25519 gives forward secrecy, HKDF derives two AES-256-GCM keys (one per direction), and the server signs the handshake with Ed25519 so the client can pin the fingerprint (TOFU) against a man-in-the-middle, as in slide 8-41 and an SSH-style pin. The 13-byte header is additional authenticated data. A replay window rejects reused packet numbers. The nonce is four zero bytes concatenated with the monotonic packet number, so it never repeats. Stream and credit limits bound memory. Chapter 8 covers Diffie-Hellman, signatures, man-in-the-middle, TLS 1.3, and the IPsec replay window.

nodes.label: Known security and scope limits
nodes.rationale: INITIAL has no anti-amplification or address-spoofing cookie and retry token of the kind QUIC uses. BBR is a reduced version 1. The finished-stream list used to stop replay is kept in RAM. Only IPv4 is supported.

nodes.label: TOFU server-key pinning
nodes.rationale: On the first connection the client pins the server fingerprint. If the key changes, the client refuses the connection to stop a man-in-the-middle. Trusting a new key means deleting that entry from known_hosts.json.

nodes.label: Per-stream ordering
nodes.rationale: Each message and each file is its own stream, so only bytes inside one stream must stay in order. A lost file packet therefore does not block chat, which is the HTTP/2 to HTTP/3 and QUIC idea from chapter 2. Chat is scheduled ahead of files, and files are round-robin. Measured chat delay is about 21 ms while a 3 MB file moves at 3 percent loss. A single TCP-style byte stream would have stalled the messages.

nodes.rationale: Network logic (common/transport.py, client/core.py, server/server.py), data processing (protocol.py, crypto.py), and the UI (client/web, plain HTML and JavaScript) are separated. The browser speaks only HTTP to a local gateway. Every packet between machines is UDP.

nodes.label: Connection resilience

nodes.label: Reliable chunked file transfer

nodes.label: Web UI
nodes.rationale: The header shows the congestion-control algorithm, RTT, congestion window, and loss in real time. Everyone is the broadcast room; selecting a person sends a private message. Files are sent only to one person, via the paperclip or drag-and-drop.

Languages suggested are Python, Java, C++, or Go. The program must run on Windows, macOS, or Linux over localhost or a LAN IP.

nodes.label: Minimal HTTP gateway
nodes.rationale: The browser cannot speak UDP, and HTTP frameworks are forbidden, so the gateway is a minimal asyncio TCP HTTP server with a parser, server-sent events, and a streaming upload. Uploads use XHR with Content-Length. The gateway reads 64 KB at a time and awaits drain so back-pressure reaches the browser TCP connection. A custom header, X-Requested-With, plus a Host check, blocks CSRF and DNS rebinding. Path traversal is rejected. Tests cover static files, the API, SSE, streamed POST upload, download, a missing X-Requested-With, a foreign Host, and path traversal.

nodes.label: Per-message stream routing
nodes.rationale: Each chat message is its own stream, broadcast or unicast through _route_msg, so a large transfer does not head-of-line block time-sensitive messages. Async I/O uses asyncio and add_reader on a raw UDP socket.

nodes.label: Akamai
nodes.rationale: Enter-deep CDN example: about 240,000 servers in more than 120 countries (2015). Also cited for DNS query volume of about 2.2 trillion queries per day.

nodes.label: Application layer
nodes.rationale: Network apps run on end systems and communicate by messages. Network-core devices do not run user applications, which keeps app development at the edge.

nodes.label: Application-layer protocol
nodes.rationale: Defines message types, syntax, semantics, and send/respond rules. Open protocols are specified in RFCs so anyone can interoperate (HTTP, SMTP). Proprietary protocols include Zoom.

nodes.label: Authoritative DNS servers
nodes.rationale: Organization or provider servers that hold the authoritative hostname-to-IP mappings for that organization's hosts. A registrar inserts NS and A records into the TLD so resolvers can find them.

nodes.label: BitTorrent
nodes.rationale: Named example of P2P file sharing and listed again in the chapter summary as the P2P protocol studied.

nodes.label: DASH
nodes.rationale: Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP. Server stores the video as chunks at several rates, replicated on CDN nodes, and a manifest lists their URLs. The client estimates bandwidth and chooses rate, timing, and server so the buffer neither starves nor overflows. Streaming video is described as encoding plus DASH plus playout buffering.

nodes.label: Domain Name System (DNS)
nodes.rationale: Distributed hierarchical database and application-layer protocol mapping names and IP addresses. Also host aliasing, mail-server aliasing, and load distribution across replicated servers. A centralized DNS would be a single point of failure, a traffic bottleneck, distant, and hard to maintain. Comcast DNS about 600 billion queries/day; Akamai DNS about 2.2 trillion/day.

nodes.label: DNS resource records
nodes.rationale: RR format is (name, value, type, ttl). A maps a hostname to an IP address. NS names the authoritative server for a domain. CNAME maps an alias to a canonical name. MX names the SMTP server for a name. Query and reply messages share one format with identification, flags (recursion desired/available, authoritative), and question, answer, authority, and additional sections.

nodes.label: DNSSEC
nodes.rationale: Provides authentication and message integrity for DNS. Counters spoofed replies and cache poisoning (RFC 4033). Root DDoS has not succeeded to date because of filtering and because local servers cache TLD addresses.

nodes.label: FTP
nodes.rationale: File transfer application that requires no data loss, elastic throughput, and is not time sensitive. Runs over TCP. Cited as RFC 959 and as a client-server example.

nodes.label: GDPR and cookie identifiers
nodes.rationale: GDPR recital 30 (May 2018) treats online identifiers such as IP addresses and cookie IDs as capable of profiling natural persons. When cookies identify an individual they are personal data, and the user has explicit control over whether cookies are allowed.

nodes.label: HTTP
nodes.rationale: Web application-layer protocol. Browser client requests objects; Web server responds. Uses TCP, typically port 80. Stateless: the server keeps no memory of past requests because endpoint state is complex and can diverge after crashes. Request methods include GET, POST, HEAD, and PUT. Sample status codes: 200, 301, 400, 404, 505.

nodes.label: HTTP/2
nodes.rationale: RFC 7540 (2015). Methods, status codes, and most headers stay as in HTTP/1.1, but the server may send objects by client priority, push unrequested objects, and interleave frames so a large object does not block small ones. A single TCP connection still stalls every object on packet loss.

nodes.label: HTTP/3
nodes.rationale: Adds security and per-object error and congestion control over UDP, so loss on one object does not stall the others the way HTTP/2 over one TCP connection does. Shown as HTTP/2 (slimmed) over QUIC over UDP.

nodes.label: ICANN
nodes.rationale: Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers manages the root DNS domain.

nodes.label: IMAP
nodes.rationale: Internet Mail Access Protocol retrieves, deletes, and folders mail that stays on the server. SMTP only delivers into the receiver mailbox. Webmail (Gmail, Hotmail, Yahoo) uses HTTP on top of SMTP to send and IMAP or POP to retrieve.

nodes.label: Local DNS name server
nodes.rationale: Host queries go first to the ISP local DNS server, which answers from cache or forwards into the hierarchy. It does not strictly belong to the hierarchy. Find it with scutil --dns on macOS or ipconfig /all on Windows.

nodes.label: E-mail message format (RFC 2822)
nodes.rationale: RFC 2822 defines the message syntax (header lines To, From, Subject, then a blank line and ASCII body), distinct from SMTP envelope commands MAIL FROM and RCPT TO. Compared with HTML defining web documents while HTTP carries them.

nodes.label: Mail server
nodes.rationale: Holds the user mailbox and a queue of outgoing messages. The sending server is the SMTP client; the receiving server is the SMTP server.

nodes.label: Netflix Open Connect
nodes.rationale: Netflix stores copies of titles at worldwide Open Connect CDN nodes. The client uses a manifest to fetch the highest supportable rate and may switch rate or copy if the path is congested. A case study separates registration and accounting (Amazon cloud) from manifest retrieval and DASH streaming from CDN servers. With YouTube and Amazon Prime, cited as about 80% of residential ISP traffic in 2020.

nodes.label: QUIC
nodes.rationale: Quick UDP Internet Connections: application-layer protocol on UDP that establishes reliability, congestion control, authentication, and encryption in one RTT, versus serial TCP and TLS handshakes. A cached TLS session ticket allows a later 0-RTT handshake. Loss and congestion algorithms parallel TCP. Deployed on many Google servers and in Chrome and the mobile YouTube app.

nodes.label: Root DNS servers
nodes.rationale: Contact of last resort when a name server cannot resolve a name. Thirteen logical root servers, each replicated many times. The Internet could not function without them.

nodes.label: SMTP
nodes.rationale: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol pushes mail over TCP port 25 from the sending mail server to the receiving server. Three phases: handshake (HELO), transfer (MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, DATA), closure (QUIT). Persistent connections, 7-bit ASCII, message ended by CRLF.CRLF. Unlike HTTP pull, SMTP is client push; multiple objects travel in one multipart message.

nodes.label: Socket
nodes.rationale: Door between the application process and the transport protocol. The app developer controls the process side; the OS controls transport below the socket. Two socket types: UDP datagrams and TCP byte streams.

nodes.label: TCP
nodes.rationale: Reliable transport, flow control, congestion control, and connection setup between processes. Does not provide timing, minimum throughput, or security. Used by FTP, SMTP, HTTP, and streaming via DASH.

nodes.label: Top-level domain DNS servers
nodes.rationale: Responsible for .com, .org, .net, .edu, and country domains. Network Solutions is the registry for .com and .net; Educause for .edu. Bombarding TLD servers is described as more dangerous than root DDoS because local caches often bypass the root.

nodes.label: Transport Layer Security (TLS)
nodes.rationale: Vanilla TCP and UDP sockets send cleartext. TLS, implemented in the application layer via libraries that use TCP, adds encryption, data integrity, and endpoint authentication so cleartext written into the socket is encrypted on the wire.

nodes.label: UDP
nodes.rationale: Unreliable datagram transfer with no flow control, congestion control, timing, throughput guarantee, security, or connection setup. Chosen when those services are unnecessary. Also the substrate for QUIC and HTTP/3.

nodes.label: Mail user agent
nodes.rationale: Mail reader (for example Outlook or an iPhone mail client) composes, edits, and reads messages. Outgoing and incoming mail is stored on the server.

nodes.label: RFC 2822
nodes.rationale: Cited as the syntax of the e-mail message itself, as distinct from the SMTP transfer protocol.

nodes.label: RFC 3501
nodes.rationale: Cited as the IMAP specification.

nodes.label: RFC 4033
nodes.rationale: Cited for DNSSEC authentication services.

nodes.label: RFC 5321
nodes.rationale: Cited as the SMTP specification.

nodes.label: RFC 7230 and RFC 9110
nodes.rationale: Cited together as the HTTP specifications for Web documents. RFC 7231 is also named as defining HTTP, analogous to RFC 5321 for SMTP.

nodes.label: RFC 7540
nodes.rationale: Cited as the 2015 HTTP/2 specification.

nodes.label: RFC 959
nodes.rationale: Cited as the FTP specification.

nodes.label: Content distribution network
nodes.rationale: A single mega-server does not scale: it is a single point of failure, a congestion point, and a long path to distant clients. A CDN stores copies at many sites. Enter-deep pushes servers into access networks (Akamai). Bring-home uses fewer larger clusters in POPs (Limelight). OTT operation must choose which node stores content and which node and rate serve a request.

nodes.label: Client-server paradigm
nodes.rationale: Server is always-on with a permanent IP, often in data centers for scaling. Clients may be intermittent, may have dynamic IPs, and do not talk directly to each other. Examples: HTTP, IMAP, FTP.

nodes.label: Conditional GET
nodes.rationale: Browser sends If-Modified-Since with the cached copy's date so the server can skip the object. Up-to-date cache yields 304 Not Modified; a newer object yields 200 OK with the body. Avoids transmission delay and network use.

nodes.label: DNS caching
nodes.rationale: Any name server may cache a mapping and answer immediately. Entries expire after a TTL. TLD servers are typically cached locally, which also lets resolvers bypass the root. Cached data can be stale until all TTLs expire, so translation is best-effort.

nodes.label: HTTP head-of-line blocking
nodes.rationale: HTTP/1.1 pipelined GETs are answered in order, so a small object waits behind a large one, and TCP loss recovery stalls every object. That delay is why HTTP/2 divides objects into scheduled frames and why HTTP/3 moves per-object control off a single TCP connection.

nodes.label: HTTP cookies
nodes.rationale: Because HTTP itself is stateless, sites keep user state with four pieces: Set-Cookie response header, Cookie request header, a browser cookie file, and a back-end database. Uses include authorization, carts, recommendations, and webmail sessions. First-party cookies track one chosen site; third-party cookies track across sites. Firefox and Safari disable third-party tracking by default.

nodes.label: Iterated DNS query
nodes.rationale: The contacted server does not resolve the name itself. It replies with the next server to ask: I do not know this name, but ask this server. Illustrated for engineering.nyu.edu resolving gaia.cs.umass.edu via local, root, TLD, and authoritative servers.

nodes.label: Non-persistent HTTP
nodes.rationale: At most one object per TCP connection, then the connection closes. Per-object time is 2 RTT plus file transmission. Multiple objects need multiple connections, plus OS overhead; browsers often open parallel TCP connections.

nodes.label: Peer-to-peer architecture
nodes.rationale: No always-on server; peers request and provide service. Self-scalability: new peers add capacity and demand. Intermittent connectivity and changing IPs make management complex. Example: BitTorrent.

nodes.label: Persistent HTTP (HTTP/1.1)
nodes.rationale: Server leaves the TCP connection open so later objects skip a new handshake. Client can send the next request as soon as it sees a reference. As little as one RTT for all referenced objects, about half the non-persistent response time.

nodes.label: Client playout buffering
nodes.rationale: Stored video has a continuous playout constraint, but network delay varies (jitter). A client buffer and playout delay absorb that jitter so playout timing can match the original timing. Pause, seek, and loss/retransmission remain separate challenges.

nodes.label: Process addressing (IP address and port)
nodes.rationale: A host 32-bit IP address does not identify a process because many processes share a host. The identifier is IP address plus port. HTTP server port 80; mail server port 25. Example: gaia.cs.umass.edu at 128.119.245.12 port 80.

nodes.label: Recursive DNS query
nodes.rationale: Puts the burden of resolution on the contacted name server, which queries further servers itself. That can place heavy load on upper levels of the hierarchy.

nodes.label: Socket timeout (settimeout)
nodes.rationale: A process may wait on a socket reply or a timer. Python socket.settimeout arms blocking recv; if no segment arrives, recv raises a timeout exception caught by try/except. settimeout(None) clears it; settimeout(0) makes the socket non-blocking. Introduced so students practice timers before a later reliable-data-transfer assignment. select or multithreading can wait on several sockets.

nodes.label: Video coding (CBR, VBR, MPEG)
nodes.rationale: Video is a constant-rate image sequence. Spatial coding removes redundancy inside a frame; temporal coding sends differences between frames. CBR keeps a fixed encoding rate; VBR changes with the amount of redundancy. Examples: MPEG-1 about 1.5 Mbps, MPEG-2 about 3-6 Mbps, MPEG-4 about 64 Kbps-12 Mbps on the Internet.

nodes.label: Web cache (proxy server)
nodes.rationale: Satisfies requests without the origin server when the object is cached. Acts as server to the client and client to the origin. Cuts response time because the cache is closer, and cuts institutional access-link traffic. In the example, a 0.4 hit rate drops access-link utilization from 0.97 to about 0.58 and average delay to about 1.2 s, cheaper than upgrading a 1.54 Mbps link to 154 Mbps.

nodes.label: AUTH message
nodes.rationale: AUTH {user, pass} on client stream 0. A new name is registered automatically. Passwords are stored with PBKDF2-SHA256, 120000 iterations, and a salt. AUTH_OK returns the user and peers; AUTH_FAIL returns a message.

nodes.label: LAN UDP beacon discovery
nodes.rationale: A server UDP broadcast beacon lets the UI button Tim trong LAN find the server. Otherwise the client is pointed at host:port, including a LAN IP.

nodes.label: Auto-registration login
nodes.rationale: A name that does not exist yet is registered with the password just entered. The username is 2 to 24 characters and the password is at least 4 characters. The server field is host:port.

nodes.label: BBR and CUBIC requirement
nodes.rationale: Streaming congestion control must support BBR or CUBIC.

nodes.label: Selective retransmission
nodes.rationale: Retransmit only the missing segments.

nodes.label: ACK SACK frame
nodes.rationale: Type 0x04. Fields are largest (8), delay in microseconds (4), range count (1), and up to 6 [start, end] ranges, so only missing spans are resent.

nodes.label: Reliable UDP delivery
nodes.rationale: Packet numbers increase monotonically, and a retransmission gets a new number. Acknowledgements are ranges (SACK). Loss is declared by a threshold of 3 packets, a time threshold of 9/8 RTT, and a probe timeout. This follows the course text chapter 3: reliable data transfer, Go-Back-N and selective repeat, and TCP RTT estimation.

nodes.label: QUIC-style selective retransmit
nodes.rationale: As in TCP, an acknowledgement of a retransmitted packet makes the RTT sample ambiguous. Every transmission uses a fresh packet number, in the QUIC style, and the sender remembers which frames rode in which packet. When a packet is declared lost, only that byte range is requeued. The whole file is not sent again.

nodes.label: Custom UDP Transport
nodes.rationale: Messaging must be reliable, so the application does not use TCP between hosts. A QUIC-like transport on raw UDP provides multiple streams, a sliding window, ACK/SACK, selective retransmit, and a choice of CUBIC or BBR.

nodes.label: Sliding window sequencing
nodes.rationale: Monotonic sequence numbers and a window provide flow control and in-order delivery.

nodes.label: CLOSE frame
nodes.rationale: Type 0x07. Closes the connection with a code and a reason, and is sent three times.

nodes.label: DATA packet 0x10
nodes.rationale: Application packet. The packet number is 8 bytes and strictly increasing. The nonce is four zero bytes concatenated with that number. Each direction has its own key.

nodes.label: MAX_STREAM_DATA frame
nodes.rationale: Type 0x05. Grants more credit (stream id and max offset) to the sender.

nodes.label: PING frame
nodes.rationale: Type 0x06. Keep-alive every 4 seconds when idle, and the probe when a PTO fires.

nodes.label: Auto-reconnect and connection migration
nodes.rationale: PING every 4 seconds and a 20 second idle timeout run on both sides. The server drops the user and broadcasts PEERS. The client reconnects with exponential backoff and logs in again. A valid packet from a new address updates the peer address (connection migration). A duplicate login kicks the previous session. This covers unexpected loss and NAT rebinding.

nodes.label: Relay credit deadlock
nodes.rationale: The server withholds the sender's stream credit when the queue toward the receiver grows too large. A real bug: the second credit hold overwrote the previous callback, so credit was never returned and the send stream stalled forever under loss. The fix keeps a list of callbacks and releases all of them when the receiver connection closes. An end-to-end test with packet loss caught it.

nodes.label: Per-stream flow control
nodes.rationale: The receive window slides per stream through MAX_STREAM_DATA and is 512 KB. The server holds the sender's credit when the receiver is slow, which is back-pressure, matching chapter 3 flow control and rwnd.

nodes.label: Automated and browser test matrix
nodes.rationale: Unit tests cover RangeSet, frame encode and decode, ECDH, AES-GCM rejection of a tampered header, and PBKDF2. Transport tests move 4 MB cleanly, survive 5 percent loss plus reordering under CUBIC and BBR with a matching SHA-256, enforce the flow-control window, reject a server with the wrong key, and notice a disconnect. End-to-end with three clients covers login, presence, broadcast, unicast that does not leak, offline ERR, a 3 MB file, an empty file, a client that vanishes, a duplicate login, and auto-reconnect, including a link with 4 percent loss and 15 ms delay under BBR. Chromium drove two users through chat, a private message, and a 4 MB file whose download matched SHA-256, with zero JavaScript errors. Every listed group passed.

nodes.label: Unittest suite
nodes.rationale: python -m unittest discover -s tests -t . -v runs 19 tests and takes about 45 seconds.

nodes.label: CUBIC and BBR with pacing
nodes.rationale: CUBIC is the default; BBR is selected with --cc bbr, and both are paced. On a 2 MB transfer at 20 ms simulated RTT with no loss, CUBIC reaches 51.76 Mbps and BBR 38.17 Mbps, because CUBIC slow-start is more aggressive. At 1, 3, and 5 percent loss CUBIC drops to 6.46, 2.78, and 2.43 Mbps because each loss multiplies the window by 0.7, while BBR stays near 37.33, 26.89, and 29.17 Mbps using a bandwidth and RTT model. Chapter 3 contrasts that loss-based and model-based control. The algorithm is a parameter for that reason. The shipped BBR is a reduced version 1.
