nodes.label: Address Resolution Protocol
nodes.rationale: Each IP node keeps an ARP table of IP address, MAC address, and TTL (typically 20 minutes). If the target MAC is missing, the sender broadcasts an ARP query to FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF; the target replies unicast with its MAC, and the sender caches the mapping.

nodes.label: Broadcast Link
nodes.rationale: Shared wire or medium: old-school Ethernet, upstream HFC, 802.11 wireless LAN, and 4G/5G or satellite radio.

nodes.label: Cyclic Redundancy Check
nodes.rationale: Sender chooses r CRC bits R so that D followed by R is divisible by generator G (mod 2). A nonzero remainder at the receiver means an error. Detects all burst errors shorter than r+1 bits. Used in Ethernet and 802.11 WiFi.

nodes.label: CSMA
nodes.rationale: Carrier sense multiple access: listen before transmit. If the channel is idle, send the whole frame; if busy, defer. Collisions still happen because propagation delay hides a transmission that has just started. Distance and delay set the collision probability.

nodes.label: CSMA/CA
nodes.rationale: Carrier-sense random access with collision avoidance, used by IEEE 802.11 because collision detection is hard on wireless links.

nodes.label: CSMA/CD
nodes.rationale: CSMA with collision detection aborts colliding transmissions quickly, cutting channel waste. Detection is easy on wired links and difficult on wireless links. Ethernet uses unslotted CSMA/CD.

nodes.label: Datacenter Network
nodes.rationale: Tens to hundreds of thousands of closely placed hosts for e-business, content serving, search, and data mining. Challenges are massive multi-application load, reliability, and avoiding processing, network, and data bottlenecks. Rich switch interconnection gives multiple paths and redundancy. Related services are placed in the same or a nearby rack to limit traffic through higher tiers.

nodes.label: DHCP
nodes.rationale: In the web-request walkthrough, a newly attached host broadcasts a DHCP request inside UDP, IP, and 802.3 Ethernet (destination FFFFFFFFFFFF). The router DHCP server returns the client IP, first-hop router IP, and DNS server name and IP. The reply is forwarded using switch learning.

nodes.label: DNS
nodes.rationale: After the first-hop MAC is known, a DNS query for www.google.com is encapsulated in UDP, IP, and Ethernet, switched to the campus router, and routed across Comcast using RIP, OSPF, IS-IS, and/or BGP. The DNS server returns the web server IP address.

nodes.label: DOCSIS
nodes.rationale: Data Over Cable Service Interface Specification. FDM separates upstream and downstream channels. A downstream MAP frame assigns some upstream slots by TDM and leaves others for random-access requests that use binary backoff. The CMTS at the cable headend transmits downstream.

nodes.label: Error Correction
nodes.rationale: Receiver identifies and corrects bit errors without retransmission.

nodes.label: Error Detection
nodes.rationale: EDC bits protect data D. Detection is not 100 percent reliable; a larger EDC field yields better detection. Causes include signal attenuation and noise. The receiver may request retransmission or drop the frame.

nodes.label: Ethernet
nodes.rationale: Dominant wired LAN technology, from Bob Metcalfe's design, spanning about 10 Mbps to 400 Gbps. Connectionless and unreliable: NICs do not handshake or send ACKs or NAKs. Dropped frames are recovered only if a higher layer such as TCP provides reliable delivery. MAC is unslotted CSMA/CD with binary backoff. Bus topology (one collision domain) gave way to a switched star.

nodes.label: Ethernet Frame
nodes.rationale: Preamble (seven 10101010 bytes plus 10101011) synchronizes clocks. Then 6-byte destination and source MAC addresses, a type field that demultiplexes the network protocol (mostly IP; also Novell IPX or AppleTalk), payload, and CRC. A mismatched unicast destination is discarded; a CRC error drops the frame.

nodes.label: Ethernet Switch
nodes.rationale: Link-layer store-and-forward device. Transparent and plug-and-play. Each host link is its own collision domain and can run full duplex, so pairs of flows transmit simultaneously. A switch table maps MAC address, outgoing interface, and timestamp. Unknown destinations are flooded; known destinations are forwarded or filtered. Interconnected switches learn the same way. Unlike a router, a switch examines link-layer headers and learns by flooding rather than by a routing algorithm.

nodes.label: FDMA
nodes.rationale: Frequency division multiple access: the spectrum is split into bands, each station gets a fixed band, and unused transmission time in a band goes idle.

nodes.label: Link-Layer Frame
nodes.rationale: Layer-2 packet that encapsulates a datagram and adds a header and trailer so the link can carry it to the next physically adjacent node.

nodes.label: HTTP
nodes.rationale: The HTTP request is written into the TCP socket, routed as an IP datagram to www.google.com, and the HTTP reply carrying the web page is routed back and displayed.

nodes.label: IEEE 802.11
nodes.rationale: Wireless LAN broadcast medium. Uses CRC for error detection and CSMA/CA rather than CSMA/CD because wireless collision detection is difficult. Carrier sensing is harder on wireless than on wire.

nodes.label: IEEE 802.1Q
nodes.rationale: Inserts a 2-byte Tag Protocol Identifier (0x8100) and Tag Control Information (12-bit VLAN ID and 3-bit priority) into an Ethernet frame between switches, then recomputes the CRC. Trunk frames cannot be vanilla 802.1 frames because they must carry the VLAN ID.

nodes.label: IEEE 802.3
nodes.rationale: Ethernet standards share one MAC protocol and frame format while physical layers differ: copper twisted pair and fiber, including 1000BASE-T, 1000BASE-SX, 1000BASE-LX, and speeds from 2 Mbps through 10, 40, and 80 Gbps.

nodes.label: Internet Checksum
nodes.rationale: Review of transport checksum (section 3.3): one's complement sum of 16-bit words over a UDP segment including header fields and IP addresses. Equal checksums do not prove the segment is error-free.

nodes.label: Leaf-Spine Topology
nodes.rationale: Two-layer datacenter fabric: leaf switches attach to servers or racks and spine switches interconnect the leaves, providing disjoint multipath routes between racks.

nodes.label: Link Layer
nodes.rationale: Transfers a datagram from one node to a physically adjacent node over a wired or wireless link. Services include framing, link access, reliable delivery between adjacent nodes, flow control, error detection and correction, and half- or full-duplex transmission.

nodes.label: Datacenter Load Balancer
nodes.rationale: Application-layer routing: accepts external client requests, directs work inside the datacenter, and returns results while hiding internal structure from the client.

nodes.label: MAC Address
nodes.rationale: 48-bit LAN or physical or Ethernet address, burned into NIC ROM and sometimes software-settable. Identifies source and destination on one subnet, unlike a 32-bit IP address. IEEE allocates the space to manufacturers. A flat address is portable across LANs; an IP address is not.

nodes.label: MPLS
nodes.rationale: Multiprotocol label switching inserts a fixed-length label (label, Exp, S, TTL) between the Ethernet header and the IP datagram. Label-switched routers forward on the label only, using an MPLS table distinct from the IP table. The IP addresses remain. Paths may depend on source and destination, enabling traffic engineering and fast reroute over precomputed backup paths. Described as an earlier flavor of generalized forwarding.

nodes.label: Multiple Access Protocol
nodes.rationale: Distributed algorithm that decides when nodes may transmit on one shared broadcast channel. Coordination uses the channel itself; there is no out-of-band channel. A collision occurs if a node receives two or more signals at once.

nodes.label: Network Interface Card
nodes.rationale: Host link layer is implemented on-chip or in a NIC that also implements the physical layer, attaches to the host bus (for example PCI), and combines hardware, software, and firmware.

nodes.label: Orion SDN
nodes.rationale: Google SDN control plane for the internal Jupiter datacenter network and the B4 wide-area network. Intradomain routing, iBGP, and traffic engineering run as applications on Orion. CoFlow scheduling provides edge-to-edge flow control for SLAs. OpenFlow signals and monitors switches. The slides note that routing protocols, and partly congestion control, are managed by SDN.

nodes.label: Parity Checking
nodes.rationale: Single-bit even or odd parity detects single-bit errors by comparing the parity of received data bits with the received parity bit.

nodes.label: Point-to-Point Link
nodes.rationale: Dedicated link between two nodes, such as a host and an Ethernet switch, or PPP dial-up access.

nodes.label: Polling
nodes.rationale: A centralized controller invites other nodes to transmit in turn. Used with simple devices, including Bluetooth. Costs are poll overhead, latency, and a single point of failure at the master.

nodes.label: PPP
nodes.rationale: Point-to-point protocol cited as the link protocol for dial-up access.

nodes.label: Pure ALOHA
nodes.rationale: Unslotted ALOHA. Success probability is p times (1-p) to the power 2(N-1) because a node must be alone in both the previous and current frame time. Optimum efficiency is 1/(2e), about 0.18, worse than slotted ALOHA.

nodes.label: RoCE
nodes.rationale: RDMA over Converged Ethernet, a datacenter link-layer mechanism for remote DMA. Transport innovations on the same networks include ECN-based DCTCP and DCQCN, plus experiments with hop-by-hop backpressure.

nodes.label: RSVP-TE
nodes.rationale: Entry MPLS router uses RSVP-TE to install MPLS forwarding state at downstream routers. OSPF and IS-IS link-state flooding are extended to carry link bandwidth and reserved bandwidth for MPLS routing.

nodes.label: Slotted ALOHA
nodes.rationale: Equal slots, synchronized nodes, transmit only at a slot boundary. On collision, retransmit in each later slot with probability p. Maximum efficiency is 1/e, about 0.37, so at best the channel carries useful transmissions 37 percent of the time.

nodes.label: TCP
nodes.rationale: Before HTTP, the client opens a TCP socket. A SYN is inter-domain routed to the Google web server; the server replies SYNACK, completing the handshake steps shown. TCP is also the higher-layer reliable delivery that recovers data Ethernet drops.

nodes.label: TDMA
nodes.rationale: Time division multiple access: each station gets a fixed-length slot in each round. Unused slots go idle.

nodes.label: Token Passing
nodes.rationale: A control token is passed sequentially; a node transmits only while it holds the token. Used by FDDI and token ring. Costs are token overhead, latency, and failure if the token is lost.

nodes.label: Top-of-Rack Switch
nodes.rationale: Access switch, one per rack of about 20 to 40 server blades, with 100G to 400G Ethernet to the blades. Tier-2 aggregation switches connect about 16 TORs; tier-1 core switches connect about 16 tier-2 switches; border routers leave the datacenter.

nodes.label: Two-Dimensional Parity
nodes.rationale: Row and column parity detect and correct a single-bit error without retransmission.

nodes.label: Virtual Circuit
nodes.rationale: MPLS borrows the virtual-circuit idea of forwarding on a fixed identifier while still carrying a full IP datagram.

nodes.label: VLAN
nodes.rationale: A single physical LAN is one broadcast domain, so ARP, DHCP, and unknown-MAC floods cross the whole LAN and hurt scale, efficiency, security, and privacy. Port-based VLANs group switch ports into virtual switches with traffic isolation. Membership can also follow endpoint MAC addresses and can be dynamic. Forwarding between VLANs is routing. A trunk port carries multiple VLANs between switches.

nodes.label: VXLAN
nodes.rationale: Ethernet VPN, also called VXLAN. Layer-2 switches at distant sites (for example Sunnyvale and Bangalore) are connected by VTEPs. An Ethernet frame is carried inside a UDP segment inside an IP datagram so a Layer-2 network is stretched over a Layer-3 underlay.

nodes.label: RFC 7348
nodes.rationale: Cited definition of VXLAN as a tunneling scheme that overlays Layer 2 networks on Layer 3 networks and runs over existing infrastructure.

nodes.label: Binary Exponential Backoff
nodes.rationale: After the m-th collision, Ethernet picks K at random from 0 through 2^m - 1 and waits K times 512 bit times before sensing again. More collisions produce a longer backoff interval.

nodes.label: Channel Partitioning MAC
nodes.rationale: Divides the channel into time, frequency, or code pieces and gives each node a piece for exclusive use. Fair and efficient at high load, but wastes delay and bandwidth at low load because idle shares stay allocated.

nodes.label: Next-Hop Link Addressing
nodes.rationale: When A sends to B on another subnet, the IP source and destination stay A and B on every hop, while each link-layer frame uses the MAC address of the next-hop interface. A frames to router R; R reframes to B.

nodes.label: Random Access MAC
nodes.rationale: Channel is not divided. A node transmits at full rate R with no prior coordination. The protocol specifies how to detect collisions and how to recover, typically by delayed retransmission. Efficient when one node is active; collision overhead grows at high load.

nodes.label: Switch Self-Learning
nodes.rationale: On each arrival the switch records the sender MAC and incoming interface. It then looks up the destination: drop if the destination is on the arrival segment, forward on the recorded interface if known, otherwise flood on all other interfaces.

nodes.label: Taking-Turns MAC
nodes.rationale: Seeks the high-load fairness of channel partitioning and the low-load efficiency of random access. Nodes take turns, and a node with more to send may hold the turn longer. Realized by polling or token passing.

nodes.label: AIMD (Additive Increase, Multiplicative Decrease)
nodes.rationale: Senders increase the rate until loss, then decrease. Additive increase adds one MSS per RTT; multiplicative decrease cuts the rate in half on loss. The resulting sawtooth probes for bandwidth. AIMD is a distributed asynchronous algorithm shown to optimize congested flow rates network-wide and to have desirable stability properties.

nodes.label: Bandwidth-Delay Product
nodes.rationale: Ideal in-flight data for a connection is its share of bottleneck bandwidth times min_RTT. Below that product, more in-flight data does not increase RTT. Above it, arrival rate exceeds link rate, the buffer fills, and RTT grows. Loss-based TCP tends to operate at the full-buffer point.

nodes.label: BBR (Bottleneck Bandwidth and RTT)
nodes.rationale: Seeks the just-full operating point rather than the loss-based full-buffer point by regulating ninflight. Acceleration raises rate until the throughput plateau; cruising sends at the rate ACKs show the network is delivering; deceleration reduces ninflight to ease the queue and look for a lower min_RTT. Over longer intervals it drains the pipe to remeasure min_RTT.

nodes.label: Bottleneck Link
nodes.rationale: Classic TCP and CUBIC raise the sending rate until some router output queue overflows. Once that link transmits at full rate R, a higher sending rate does not raise end-to-end throughput; it increases RTT through queueing delay. With N flows, each should ideally receive R/N. The design goal is to keep the end-to-end pipe just full, but not fuller.

nodes.label: TCP Congestion Avoidance
nodes.rationale: Once cwnd exceeds ssthresh, each new ACK increases cwnd by MSS*(MSS/cwnd), which is about one MSS per RTT: linear probing rather than doubling.

nodes.label: Congestion Control
nodes.rationale: Congestion is too many sources sending too much data too fast for the network, seen as long queueing delay and loss from router buffer overflow. Costs include extra retransmission work, unneeded duplicates that waste capacity, and upstream transmission wasted when a packet is dropped downstream. Throughput cannot exceed link capacity. It is a different problem from flow control.

nodes.label: Connectionless Demultiplexing
nodes.rationale: UDP demultiplexes using only the destination port number. Datagrams with the same destination port but different source IP addresses or source ports are delivered to the same socket.

nodes.label: TCP Congestion Window (cwnd)
nodes.rationale: The sender limits transmission by LastByteSent - LastByteAcked < cwnd. cwnd is adjusted from observed congestion. Rough sending rate is cwnd/RTT bytes per second: send cwnd bytes, wait about one RTT for ACKs, then send more.

nodes.label: Demultiplexing
nodes.rationale: The receiver uses header fields to deliver a segment to the correct socket. Each IP datagram carries one transport segment; the host combines IP addresses with source and destination port numbers.

nodes.label: Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN)
nodes.rationale: Network-assisted congestion control, also exemplified by ATM and DECbit. Routers mark two bits in the IP ToS field under an operator-chosen policy. The mark is carried to the destination, which sets the ECE bit on the TCP ACK. Both IP ECN bits and TCP C,E bits are involved, so the sender learns congestion without waiting for loss. End-to-end control, used by TCP, instead infers congestion only from observed loss and delay, with no explicit network feedback.

nodes.label: TCP Fast Recovery
nodes.rationale: On a third duplicate ACK, ssthresh becomes cwnd/2, cwnd becomes ssthresh+3, and the missing segment is retransmitted. Further duplicate ACKs inflate cwnd by one MSS. A new ACK sets cwnd back to ssthresh and returns to congestion avoidance. A timeout from this state sets cwnd to 1 MSS and restarts slow start.

nodes.label: TCP Fast Retransmit
nodes.rationale: RFC 5681 ACK rules: delayed ACK up to 500 ms for a single in-order segment, an immediate cumulative ACK when a second in-order segment arrives, a duplicate ACK on a gap, and an immediate ACK when a segment fills a gap. Three duplicate ACKs mean later segments arrived, so the missing segment is likely lost and is retransmitted without waiting for timeout. A later cumulative ACK can also cover an earlier lost ACK.

nodes.label: Flow Control
nodes.rationale: Keeps one sender from overflowing one receiver's socket buffer when the network delivers data faster than the application reads it. Distinct from congestion control, which limits many senders for the network's sake.

nodes.label: TCP Four-Tuple Demultiplexing
nodes.rationale: A TCP socket is identified by source IP, source port, destination IP, and destination port. A server can hold many simultaneous sockets, and segments that share a destination IP and port (for example port 80) are demultiplexed to different sockets using the full 4-tuple.

nodes.label: Go-Back-N
nodes.rationale: Sender window of up to N consecutive unACKed packets with a k-bit sequence number. Cumulative ACK(n) acknowledges all packets through n and slides the window to n+1. One timer runs for the oldest in-flight packet; timeout(n) retransmits packet n and every higher packet still in the window. Receiver ACKs only the highest in-order packet (rcv_base) and may discard or buffer out-of-order packets; the extended FSM discards them and needs only expectedseqnum.

nodes.label: HTTP/3
nodes.rationale: Runs over UDP via QUIC. When reliable transfer is needed over UDP, reliability and congestion control are added at the application layer rather than by TCP. The stack contrast is HTTP/2 over TCP plus TLS versus a slimmed HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 over UDP and QUIC.

nodes.label: Internet Checksum
nodes.rationale: Detects flipped bits. The sender treats the UDP segment, including header fields and IP addresses, as 16-bit integers and stores the one's complement sum, with end-around carry, in the checksum field. The receiver recomputes it. Equality does not prove the segment is error-free: some bit flips leave the checksum unchanged, so protection is weak.

nodes.label: Multiplexing
nodes.rationale: At the sender, data from multiple sockets is gathered and a transport header is added so the receiver can later demultiplex each segment to the correct socket.

nodes.label: Pipelining
nodes.rationale: The sender allows multiple in-flight, not-yet-acknowledged packets. Sequence-number range must grow and sender and/or receiver must buffer. Three-packet pipelining multiplies the stop-and-wait utilization example by about three.

nodes.label: QUIC (Quick UDP Internet Connections)
nodes.rationale: Application-layer protocol on UDP that takes on connection establishment, error control, and congestion control to speed HTTP. Many application streams share one QUIC connection, each with its own reliable transfer, while congestion control is common, so a loss does not head-of-line block other streams the way TCP reliable delivery does under HTTP/1.1. Reliability, congestion control, authentication, encryption, and state can be established in one RTT or even zero. Deployed on many Google servers and apps, including Chrome and the mobile YouTube app. The QUIC specification notes that its loss detection and congestion control parallel well-known TCP algorithms.

nodes.label: rdt1.0
nodes.rationale: Reliable transfer over a perfectly reliable channel: no bit errors and no packet loss. The sender puts data on the channel and the receiver reads it. Separate FSMs, no ACKs or retransmission.

nodes.label: rdt2.0
nodes.rationale: Channel may flip bits. Checksum detects errors. ACK means the packet was received OK; NAK means it had errors and the sender retransmits. Stop-and-wait: send one packet, then wait for the receiver response. A corrupted ACK or NAK is a fatal flaw because the sender cannot safely retransmit without risking duplicates.

nodes.label: rdt2.1
nodes.rationale: Handles garbled ACK/NAK by adding a sequence number. Alternating sequence numbers 0 and 1 suffice for stop-and-wait. The sender retransmits the current packet if ACK/NAK is corrupted; the receiver discards duplicates. Sender state must remember which sequence number is outstanding, so there are twice as many states. The receiver still cannot know whether its last ACK/NAK arrived.

nodes.label: rdt2.2
nodes.rationale: NAK-free equivalent of rdt2.1. Instead of a NAK, the receiver ACKs the last packet received OK and includes that sequence number. A duplicate ACK causes the sender to retransmit the current packet. TCP uses this approach.

nodes.label: rdt3.0
nodes.rationale: The channel can also lose data and ACKs. Checksums, sequence numbers, and ACKs are not enough. The sender starts a countdown timer and retransmits if no ACK arrives in a reasonable time. A delayed packet or ACK produces a duplicate, which sequence numbers already handle, so the ACK must name the packet. Stop-and-wait utilization is very low (example: 1 Gbps, 15 ms delay, 8000-bit packet yields Usender about 0.00027) because the protocol waits an RTT per packet.

nodes.label: TCP Receive Window (rwnd)
nodes.rationale: The receiver advertises free buffer space in the rwnd header field. RcvBuffer is set by socket options, typically defaulting to 4096 bytes, and many operating systems auto-adjust it. The sender limits unACKed in-flight data to the advertised rwnd so the receive buffer does not overflow.

nodes.label: Reliable Data Transfer
nodes.rationale: Application sees a reliable channel even though the network channel may lose, corrupt, or reorder data. Sender and receiver do not know each other's state unless it is communicated. Complexity of the rdt protocol depends on the unreliable channel. Interfaces are rdt_send, udt_send, rdt_rcv, and deliver_data. FSMs specify the protocol; data is unidirectional while control flows both ways.

nodes.label: TCP RTT Estimation and TimeoutInterval
nodes.rationale: Timeout must exceed RTT. Too short causes premature retransmission; too long reacts slowly to loss. SampleRTT measures transmission to ACK, ignoring retransmissions. EstimatedRTT is an EWMA with typical alpha 0.125. DevRTT is an EWMA of the absolute deviation with typical beta 0.25. TimeoutInterval = EstimatedRTT + 4*DevRTT so the safety margin grows when RTT varies.

nodes.label: Selective Repeat
nodes.rationale: Receiver individually ACKs every correctly received packet and buffers out-of-order packets for in-order delivery. Sender keeps a timer per unACKed packet and retransmits only the packet that timed out, with at most N in flight. If the window is too large for the sequence space (example: sequence numbers 0-3 and window 3), a retransmission can fall inside the receiver window and be accepted as new data, because the receiver cannot see the sender's state.

nodes.label: TCP Slow Start
nodes.rationale: At connection start cwnd is 1 MSS and doubles every RTT by incrementing cwnd on every ACK, so the initial rate is slow but the ramp is exponential. Growth switches to linear when cwnd reaches ssthresh, set on a loss event to half the cwnd just before the loss. The initial ssthresh shown in the FSM is 64 KB.

nodes.label: SNMP
nodes.rationale: Used as the running example of UDP sender and receiver actions: the SNMP message is placed in a UDP segment, passed to IP, checksum-checked, and demultiplexed to the socket.

nodes.label: Stop-and-Wait
nodes.rationale: The sender transmits one packet and waits for the receiver response before sending another. Correct but limits utilization of a high-bandwidth, long-delay channel to a small fraction of capacity.

nodes.label: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)
nodes.rationale: Connection-oriented, point-to-point, full-duplex reliable in-order byte stream with no message boundaries. Handshake initializes sender and receiver state. Congestion control and flow control together set the pipeline window. MSS is the maximum segment size.

nodes.label: TCP Connection Teardown
nodes.rationale: Each side closes by sending a segment with FIN=1 and ACKing the peer's FIN. An ACK may be combined with its own FIN, and simultaneous FINs are allowed. The closing FSM uses FIN_WAIT_1, FIN_WAIT_2, CLOSE_WAIT, LAST_ACK, CLOSING path states, and TIMED_WAIT for twice the maximum segment lifetime before CLOSED.

nodes.label: TCP CUBIC
nodes.rationale: Probes usable bandwidth using Wmax, the window at which congestion loss was last detected. After cutting the window in half, CUBIC increases W as a cubic function of the distance between the current time and K, the tunable time at which the window would again reach Wmax: larger steps far from K, smaller steps near K. It was the default in Linux and the most popular TCP on popular web servers until about 2024.

nodes.label: TCP Fairness
nodes.rationale: If K TCP sessions share a bottleneck of bandwidth R, each should average R/K. Two sessions with additive increase of slope 1 and multiplicative decrease converge to equal shares under idealized assumptions: same RTT, fixed number of sessions, and congestion avoidance only. Fairness is not enforced: UDP multimedia can send at a constant rate and tolerate loss, and an application can open many parallel TCP connections (one connection gets R/10 beside nine others; eleven connections get about R/2). There is no Internet police for congestion control.

nodes.label: TCP Reno
nodes.rationale: On loss detected by a triple duplicate ACK, the sending rate is cut in half. Timeout still collapses the window to 1 MSS.

nodes.label: TCP Segment Structure
nodes.rationale: Header fields include source and destination ports, sequence number (bytes in the bytestream, not segments), acknowledgement number (next expected byte, with the A bit), header length, receive window, Internet checksum, urgent pointer, options, and flags RST, SYN, FIN for connection management plus C and E for congestion notification.

nodes.label: TCP Sequence Numbers and Cumulative ACKs
nodes.norm_label: tcp sequence numbers and cumulative acks
nodes.rationale: Sequence number is the byte-stream number of the first data byte in the segment. An ACK carries the next byte expected from the other side and is cumulative. The telnet example shows Host A sending 'C' at Seq=42, ACK=79 and Host B echoing it at Seq=79, ACK=43. How the receiver treats out-of-order segments is not specified; it is up to the implementor.

nodes.label: TCP Tahoe
nodes.rationale: On loss detected by timeout, the sending rate is cut to 1 MSS rather than halved.

nodes.label: TCP Three-Way Handshake
nodes.rationale: Before data, both sides agree to connect and agree on parameters such as initial sequence numbers. Client sends SYN (Seq=x) and enters SYN_SENT; server replies SYN-ACK (Seq=y, ACKnum=x+1) and enters SYN_RCVD; client sends ACK (ACKnum=y+1), which may carry data, and both reach ESTAB. Each ACK shows the other endpoint is live. Illustrated by the climbing exchange: On belay? / Belay on. / Climbing.

nodes.label: Transport Layer
nodes.rationale: Provides logical communication between application processes on different hosts. The sender segments application messages and passes them to the network layer; the receiver reassembles segments and delivers them via sockets. Internet transport offers multiplexing, reliable data transfer, flow control, and congestion control, but not delay or bandwidth guarantees.

nodes.label: Two-Way Handshake
nodes.rationale: req_conn(x) followed by acc_conn(x) does not always work. Variable delay, retransmission after loss, and reordering can leave a half-open connection with no client, or cause the server to accept duplicate data after it has forgotten x. Neither side can see the other.

nodes.label: UDP (User Datagram Protocol)
nodes.rationale: Connectionless best-effort transport: segments may be lost or reordered, there is no handshake (so no extra RTT), no connection state, a small header, and no congestion control, so the sender can transmit as fast as desired and still function when the network is congested. Reliability and congestion control, if needed, are added in the application (as in HTTP/3).

nodes.label: UDP Segment Header
nodes.rationale: Four fields: source port, destination port, length in bytes of the UDP segment including the header, and checksum, followed by the application payload.

nodes.label: Kelly congestion-control optimality result
nodes.rationale: Cited for the result that AIMD optimizes congested flow rates network-wide and has desirable stability properties. The slides name Kelly without a year or title.

nodes.label: Mathis 1997 TCP throughput model
nodes.rationale: Average TCP throughput is about 3/4 W per RTT when loss occurs at window W, ignoring slow start. In terms of segment loss probability L, throughput is about 1.22 * MSS / (RTT * sqrt(L)). A 10 Gbps target with 1500-byte segments and 100 ms RTT needs on the order of 83,333 in-flight segments and a loss rate of about 2e-10, which motivates TCP versions for long, high-speed pipes.

nodes.label: RFC 5681
nodes.rationale: Cited specifically for TCP receiver ACK generation, including delayed ACKs and duplicate ACKs.

nodes.label: TCP RFCs 793, 1122, 2018, 5681, and 7323
nodes.rationale: The overview of TCP points to these RFCs for the protocol, host requirements, selective acknowledgement, congestion control, and window scale.

nodes.label: Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (9th edition)
nodes.norm_label: computer networking: a top-down approach (9th edition)
nodes.rationale: Pearson 2025 textbook by Jim Kurose and Keith Ross. These slides are copyright 1996-2025 J.F. Kurose and K.W. Ross and are the Chapter 3 lecture deck.

nodes.label: ATM CBR and ABR
nodes.rationale: ATM Constant Bit Rate guarantees a constant rate, no loss, order, and timing. Available Bit Rate guarantees a minimum bandwidth and order but not timing.

nodes.label: CIDR
nodes.rationale: Classless InterDomain Routing. The subnet portion has arbitrary length. Address format a.b.c.d/x, where x is the number of bits in the subnet portion (example 200.23.16.0/23).

nodes.label: DHCP
nodes.rationale: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol lets a host obtain an address when it joins, renew a lease, reuse addresses, and support mobile users (plug-and-play). Four messages: discover, offer, request, ack. Discover and offer may be skipped if the client reuses a previous address (RFC 2131). Also returns the first-hop router, DNS server name and address, and network mask. Often co-located in the router. DHCP is carried in UDP in IP in Ethernet and broadcast on the LAN (ports 68 and 67; Ethernet broadcast FFFFFFFFFFFF).

nodes.label: Diffserv
nodes.rationale: Differentiated services (RFC 2475) with possible bandwidth, loss, and order guarantees. The IPv4 type-of-service field uses bits 0-5 for Diffserv and bits 6-7 for ECN.

nodes.label: FCFS Scheduling
nodes.rationale: First-come, first-served, also called FIFO: packets leave the output port in arrival order.

nodes.label: Firewall
nodes.rationale: In the OpenFlow abstraction, a firewall matches IP addresses and TCP/UDP port numbers and permits or denies. Examples drop all datagrams to TCP port 22 and all datagrams from host 128.119.1.1. Deployed by enterprises, institutions, service providers, and ISPs, often with IDS.

nodes.label: Flow Table
nodes.rationale: A flow is defined by header field values across link, network, and transport layers. Each rule has a match pattern (wildcards allowed), an action, a priority to disambiguate overlapping patterns, and counters of bytes and packets. Orchestrated tables across switches produce network-wide behavior.

nodes.label: Head-of-the-Line Blocking
nodes.rationale: If the fabric is slower than the combined input ports, input queues form. A datagram at the front blocked by output-port contention prevents later datagrams in that queue from moving, causing delay and loss on overflow.

nodes.label: ICANN
nodes.rationale: Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (icann.org) allocates IP address blocks through five regional registries, which may allocate to local registries, and manages the DNS root zone including TLD delegation.

nodes.label: ICMP
nodes.rationale: Network-layer protocol for error reporting and router signaling, shown beside IP and the forwarding table.

nodes.label: Intserv Guaranteed Service
nodes.rationale: Internet service model in RFC 1633 offering bandwidth, loss, order, and timing guarantees, contrasted with best effort.

nodes.label: IPv4 Datagram
nodes.rationale: Header includes version, header length, type of service (Diffserv and ECN), total length, identification, flags, fragment offset, TTL decremented at each router, upper-layer protocol, header checksum, 32-bit source and destination addresses, and optional options. Typical size is 1500 bytes or less; maximum is 64K. A 20-byte IP header plus 20-byte TCP header is 40 bytes before application data.

nodes.label: IP Fragmentation and Reassembly
nodes.rationale: A datagram larger than a link MTU is split inside the network and reassembled only at the destination. Identification, fragment offset, and flags order the pieces. Example: a 4000-byte datagram over a 1500-byte MTU becomes fragments of 1500, 1500, and 1040 bytes, with offsets in 8-byte units (0, 185, 370) because 1480/8 = 185.

nodes.label: IP Protocol
nodes.rationale: Internet network-layer protocol present in every host and router. Defines datagram format, addressing, and packet-handling conventions. The sender encapsulates transport segments into datagrams; the receiver delivers segments up to the transport protocol.

nodes.label: IPv4 Addressing
nodes.rationale: A 32-bit identifier for each host or router interface, written in dotted-decimal notation. An interface connects a host or router to a physical link. Routers typically have many interfaces; hosts typically have one or two (Ethernet and 802.11). Vint Cerf is quoted on the choice of 32 bits. ICANN allocated the last IPv4 chunks to regional registries in 2011.

nodes.label: IPv6
nodes.rationale: Motivated by IPv4 exhaustion, by faster forwarding with a 40-byte fixed header, and by per-flow treatment. 128-bit addresses, priority, flow label, payload length, next header, and hop limit. No checksum, no fragmentation or reassembly, and no options (options move to a next-header protocol). Google reported about 40 percent of clients using IPv6 in 2023; NIST reported one third of US government domains IPv6-capable. Deployment has taken more than 25 years.

nodes.label: IPv6 Tunneling
nodes.rationale: Transition without a flag day: an IPv6 datagram is carried as the payload of an IPv4 datagram between IPv4 routers (packet within a packet). Tunneling is also used extensively in 4G/5G. The outer IPv4 header uses the tunnel endpoints; the inner IPv6 header keeps the original source and destination.

nodes.label: Middlebox
nodes.rationale: RFC 3234: any intermediary on the path that does more than the normal functions of an IP router. Examples: NAT (home, cellular, institutional), firewalls and IDS, load balancers, caches and CDNs, and application-specific boxes. Originally proprietary hardware; the trend is white-box hardware, open APIs, match-plus-action, and software differentiation. Described as the IP hourglass's middle-age love handles.

nodes.label: MTU
nodes.rationale: Maximum transfer unit: the largest link-level frame a network link can carry. Different link types have different MTUs, which forces IP fragmentation of oversized datagrams.

nodes.label: NAT
nodes.rationale: Network address translation lets every device in a local network share one public IPv4 address. The NAT router rewrites the source (IP, port) of outgoing datagrams, records the pair in a translation table, and rewrites the destination of incoming datagrams. Advantages: one ISP address, internal renumbering and ISP changes stay local, and inside hosts are not directly addressable. Controversial because routers process above layer 3, it was argued IPv6 should solve the shortage, it violates the end-to-end argument by manipulating port numbers, and NAT traversal is hard for inbound connections. Widely used in home, institutional, and 4G/5G networks.

nodes.label: Network Functions Virtualization
nodes.rationale: Programmable network services running over white-box networking, computation, and storage, paired with SDN's centralized control and configuration.

nodes.label: OpenFlow
nodes.rationale: Flow-table entries match link-layer fields (ingress port, source and destination MAC, Ethertype, VLAN id and priority), network-layer fields (IP ToS, protocol, source and destination), and transport ports. Actions: forward to ports, drop, modify headers, or encapsulate and send to the controller. Packet and byte counters are kept. Examples include destination-based forwarding, blocking TCP port 22, and blocking a specific source host.

nodes.label: P4
nodes.rationale: A more general form of per-packet network programming than match-plus-action, cited via p4.org, following the historical line of active networking.

nodes.label: Priority Scheduling
nodes.rationale: Traffic is classified into priority classes. The scheduler always sends from the highest non-empty queue, with FCFS inside a class. Tied to who gets the best performance and to network-neutrality concerns about paid prioritization.

nodes.label: Private IP Address Space
nodes.rationale: Prefixes 10/8, 172.16/12, and 192.168/16 are usable only inside the local network. The running example uses 10.0.0/24 inside and 138.76.29.7 as the single public NAT address.

nodes.label: RFC 1958 Architectural Principles
nodes.rationale: The goal is connectivity, the tool is the Internet Protocol, and the intelligence is end to end rather than hidden in the network. Three cornerstone beliefs: simple connectivity, IP as the narrow waist, and complexity at the edge.

nodes.label: RFC 3439 Buffering Rule
nodes.rationale: Rule of thumb: average buffering equal to a typical RTT (about 250 ms) times link capacity C. Example: a 10 Gbps link implies a 2.5 Gbit buffer. A later recommendation with N flows is RTT times C over square root of N.

nodes.label: Round Robin Scheduling
nodes.rationale: The server cyclically scans class queues and sends one complete packet from each class that has a packet.

nodes.label: Router Architecture
nodes.rationale: Input ports, high-speed switching fabric, output ports, and a routing processor. Forwarding is decentralized in port hardware; routing and management stay in the control-plane processor.

nodes.label: Routing
nodes.rationale: Determine the route packets take from source to destination using routing algorithms. Analogy: planning a trip, distinct from per-hop forwarding.

nodes.label: OSPF and BGP
nodes.rationale: Path-selection algorithms implemented in routing protocols (OSPF, BGP) or, alternatively, in an SDN controller. They fill the forwarding table used by the data plane.

nodes.label: Software-Defined Networking
nodes.rationale: A remote controller, rather than a routing process in every router, computes forwarding tables and installs them. Control is logically centralized, often in a private or public cloud, while match-plus-action remains the local data-plane mechanism.

nodes.label: Subnet
nodes.rationale: Device interfaces that can reach each other without an intervening router. Detaching interfaces from hosts and routers leaves isolated islands, each a subnet. High-order bits are the subnet part; low-order bits are the host part. A /24 mask means the high-order 24 bits identify the subnet.

nodes.label: Switching Fabric
nodes.rationale: Transfers packets from input links to output links. Three types: via memory (CPU, two bus crossings, limited by memory bandwidth), via a shared bus (contention; 32 Gbps Cisco 5600 sufficient for access routers), and via an interconnection network (crossbar, Clos, multistage; cells switched in parallel). Cisco CRS uses 8 switching planes, each a 3-stage network, up to hundreds of Tbps. Desired rate is N times line rate.

nodes.label: TCAM
nodes.rationale: Ternary content-addressable memory: present an address and retrieve the matching forwarding entry in one clock cycle independent of table size.

nodes.label: Weighted Fair Queuing
nodes.rationale: Generalized round robin. Class i with weight wi receives a weighted share wi over the sum of weights each cycle, giving a minimum bandwidth guarantee per traffic class.

nodes.label: Chapter 4 Network Layer Data Plane
nodes.rationale: Kurose and Ross, Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach, 9th edition (Pearson, 2025), slides on the network-layer data plane: service models, router internals, IP, NAT, IPv6, generalized forwarding, and middleboxes.

nodes.label: Internet Best-Effort Service
nodes.rationale: No guarantees of successful delivery, timing or order, or bandwidth. Simplicity enabled wide deployment; bandwidth provisioning, nearby replicated services (datacenters and CDNs), and congestion control of elastic traffic make performance good enough most of the time.

nodes.label: Buffer Management
nodes.rationale: When output buffers fill because the fabric delivers faster than the link can send, a drop policy chooses victims: tail drop or priority drop. Marking (ECN, RED) signals congestion without necessarily dropping. Excess buffering, especially in home routers, increases delay and hurts real-time apps and delay-based congestion control.

nodes.label: Control Plane
nodes.rationale: Network-wide logic that chooses the end-to-end path. Two approaches: traditional routing algorithms inside each router, or software-defined networking where a remote controller computes and installs forwarding tables. How tables are computed is deferred to the next chapter.

nodes.label: Data Plane
nodes.rationale: Local, per-router function that decides which output port an arriving datagram uses. Implemented in forwarding hardware and operates on a nanosecond timescale, separate from millisecond-scale control-plane software.

nodes.label: End-to-End Argument
nodes.rationale: Saltzer, Reed, and Clark (1981): a function such as reliable transfer or congestion control can be completely and correctly implemented only with the knowledge of the application at the endpoints, so it cannot be provided solely as a feature of the communication system. An incomplete in-network version may still help performance. The slides contrast the 20th-century phone network (intelligence in switches), the pre-2005 Internet (intelligence at the edge), and the post-2005 Internet (programmable devices plus massive edge infrastructure).

nodes.label: Forwarding
nodes.rationale: Move packets from a router's input link to the appropriate output link. Analogy: getting through a single interchange, as opposed to planning the whole trip (routing).

nodes.label: IP Hourglass
nodes.rationale: The Internet's thin waist is a single network-layer protocol, IP, implemented by every connected device, with many protocols above (TCP, UDP, HTTP, SMTP, QUIC, DASH, RTP) and below (Ethernet, WiFi, Bluetooth, PPP, PDCP, copper, radio, fiber). Middleboxes operating inside the network are called the architecture's middle-age love handles.

nodes.label: Longest Prefix Matching
nodes.rationale: Destination-based forwarding selects the forwarding-table entry whose address prefix is the longest match. Needed so a more-specific route can override an aggregated prefix. Often done in TCAM in one clock cycle regardless of table size; a Cisco Catalyst holds about 1M entries.

nodes.label: Match Plus Action
nodes.rationale: Generalized forwarding matches bits in arriving headers and takes an action: drop, forward, modify, copy, log, or send to a controller. Many header fields can matter, unlike destination-IP-only forwarding. The same abstraction unifies a router (longest prefix, forward), a switch (destination MAC, forward or flood), a firewall (addresses and ports, permit or deny), and NAT (address and port, rewrite). It is a simple form of network programmability, with roots in active networking; P4 is the more general programming model today.

nodes.label: Network Neutrality
nodes.rationale: How an ISP should share resources, technically via scheduling and buffer management, and socially via speech, innovation, and competition. The 2015 US FCC Open Internet order set three bright-line rules: no blocking, no throttling, and no paid prioritization, subject to reasonable network management. The order was rolled back in 2017 and that rollback was itself rolled back in 2024. Whether an ISP is a Title II telecommunications service (common-carrier duties) or a Title I information service under the Communications Acts of 1934 and 1996 determines how strongly it is regulated.

nodes.label: Packet Scheduling
nodes.rationale: Decides which queued packet is sent next on a link. Policies: first-come-first-served, priority, round robin, and weighted fair queueing. Classification may use any header fields. These mechanisms, with buffer management, are how an ISP allocates resources.

nodes.label: Route Aggregation
nodes.rationale: Hierarchical allocation lets an ISP advertise one prefix for many customer blocks (Fly-By-Night-ISP advertises 200.23.16.0/20 covering eight /23 organizations). When Organization 1 moves to ISPs-R-Us, that ISP advertises the more-specific 200.23.18.0/23, which is why longest-prefix match is required.

nodes.label: RFC 1723
nodes.rationale: Cited as the RIP specification.

nodes.label: RFC 2328
nodes.rationale: Cited as the OSPF specification.

nodes.label: RFC 4371
nodes.rationale: Cited by the slides for BGP messages OPEN, UPDATE, KEEPALIVE, and NOTIFICATION.

nodes.label: RFC 7868
nodes.rationale: Cited for EIGRP becoming an open protocol in 2013.

nodes.label: AES
nodes.rationale: Advanced Encryption Standard, the symmetric NIST standard that replaced DES in November 2001. Processes 128-bit blocks with 128-, 192-, or 256-bit keys. The slides contrast brute-force cost with DES to show the larger key space. Also the session cipher for WPA2 and the basis of four TLS 1.3 cipher suites.

nodes.label: Application Gateway
nodes.rationale: Filters on application data as well as IP, TCP, and UDP fields. An authorized user connects to the gateway, which opens a second connection to the destination and relays between them, while the packet filter blocks that application unless it originates at the gateway. Client software must be configured to contact the gateway.

nodes.label: Authentication Header
nodes.rationale: IPsec protocol, RFC 4302. Provides source authentication and data integrity but not confidentiality. Less widely used than ESP.

nodes.label: Certification Authority
nodes.rationale: Binds an entity (person, website, or router) to its public key after a proof of identity, and signs that certificate with the CA private key. Relying parties apply the CA public key to learn the entity's public key. This is the chapter's fix for public-key authentication that would otherwise accept an unverified key.

nodes.label: Cryptographic Hash Function
nodes.rationale: Many-to-one function that produces a fixed-size message digest. Given only the digest, finding a message with that digest is computationally infeasible. Used so a digital signature can cover a short fingerprint instead of a long message, and so TLS can provide integrity.

nodes.label: Denial of Service
nodes.rationale: A named threat: prevent a service from being used by others, for example by overloading resources. The chapter lists it among what an intruder can do, as a reason for firewalls, and as something an intrusion detection system can look for. Other named threats in the same overview, without procedures here, are eavesdropping, inserting messages, impersonation by spoofing a source address, and hijacking a connection.

nodes.label: DES
nodes.rationale: Data Encryption Standard, the US NIST 1993 symmetric standard: 56-bit key, 64-bit block cipher with cipher block chaining. The DES Challenge showed a 56-bit key can be searched in less than a day; the slides claim no known good analytic attack.

nodes.label: Diffie-Hellman
nodes.rationale: Public-key agreement distinct from RSA. Each side combines its own private value with the other's public value so both compute the same shared secret without sending that secret. TLS 1.3 requires Diffie-Hellman for key exchange.

nodes.label: Digital Signature
nodes.rationale: The sender signs with the private key; anyone with the public key can verify, and the signer cannot later deny the signature (non-repudiation). In practice the signature is the private-key encryption of a hash, which also detects a changed message.

nodes.label: Extensible Authentication Protocol
nodes.rationale: Framework for enterprise Wi-Fi authentication, primarily between the client and an authentication server, with the access point as a pass-through. About 40 methods differ by credential (passwords, certificates, SIM cards, tokens). The slides name EAP-MD5, EAP-TLS, EAP-PEAP, EAP-TTLS, EAP-FAST, and Cisco LEAP. EAPOL carries EAP over the LAN. 802.1X roles are supplicant (client), authenticator (access point), and authentication server.

nodes.label: EAP-TTLS
nodes.rationale: Tunneled Transport Layer Security, RFC 5281. Phase 1: the client authenticates the authentication server (for example with the server public key) and a TLS tunnel is established. Phase 2: the server authenticates the client credential inside that tunnel, then the tunnel is removed. A later four-way EAPOL handshake encrypts the wireless channel; it is not the authentication step.

nodes.label: Encapsulating Security Payload
nodes.rationale: IPsec protocol, RFC 4303. Provides source authentication, data integrity, and confidentiality, and is more widely used than AH. The ESP header carries the SPI and a sequence number; the trailer pads for block ciphers; the authentication field holds a MAC under the SA's shared key.

nodes.label: Firewall
nodes.rationale: Isolates an administered network from the public Internet, passing some packets and blocking others. Goals stated in the chapter: limit denial-of-service resource exhaustion, prevent unauthorized modification of internal data, and allow only authorized access. Three types: stateless packet filters, stateful packet filters, and application gateways. Limits: a filter cannot be sure a source address is genuine, UDP policy is often all-or-nothing, each special application may need its own gateway, and more connectivity with the outside means less isolation.

nodes.label: 5G Authentication
nodes.rationale: A visiting UE associates with a base station and mutually authenticates with the network. The SIM provides a global identity and shared keys known to the UE and the home network. The visited AMF/SEAF reaches the home AUSF over a TLS tunnel; the home UDM builds an authentication token and an expected response; the UE checks the token and returns its response; the home AUSF, not the visited network, compares them (a change from the 4G MME). On success the home AUSF sends an anchor key to the visited AMF, and the device derives the same anchor key to protect traffic in the visited network, including the gNB. Service in the visited network depends on the home subscription.

nodes.label: HTTPS
nodes.rationale: HTTP protected by TLS, cited as the browser and server use of TLS on port 443. TLS itself is an API any application can use, not only HTTP.

nodes.label: Internet Key Exchange
nodes.rationale: Replaces manual IPsec keys, which do not scale to a VPN with hundreds of endpoints. Peers authenticate with a pre-shared key or with public keys and certificates, then agree algorithms, keys, and SPI values. Phase 1 builds a bidirectional IKE SA (also called an ISAKMP SA), distinct from an IPsec SA. Phase 2 uses that SA to negotiate a pair of IPsec SAs. Aggressive mode uses fewer messages; main mode provides identity protection and more flexibility. The public-key path is described as similar to an SSL handshake.

nodes.label: Internet Checksum
nodes.rationale: Fixed-length 16-bit many-to-one digest, but another message with the same checksum is easy to find, so it is a poor cryptographic hash and does not provide message integrity.

nodes.label: Intrusion Detection System
nodes.rationale: Goes beyond header-only packet filters by inspecting packet contents (for example against a database of known malicious strings) and by correlating multiple packets. The chapter names port scanning, network mapping, and denial of service as patterns an IDS can examine. Sensors may sit at different places, including beside a firewall and a demilitarized zone.

nodes.label: IPsec
nodes.rationale: Network-layer security providing datagram encryption, authentication, and integrity for user traffic and for control traffic such as BGP and DNS. Peers can be two end systems, two routers or firewalls, or one of each. IP is connectionless, but IPsec is connection-oriented via security associations. A security policy database says what to do for a datagram; a security association database says how, looked up by the SPI.

nodes.label: IPsec Transport Mode
nodes.rationale: Only the datagram payload is encrypted and authenticated; the original IP header stays outside that protection.

nodes.label: IPsec Tunnel Mode
nodes.rationale: The entire original datagram, header included, is encrypted and authenticated, then encapsulated in a new datagram with a new IP header and tunneled to the tunnel endpoint. This hides the original source and destination from an on-path observer who does not have the keys.

nodes.label: MD5
nodes.rationale: Hash widely used under RFC 1321. Computes a 128-bit digest in a four-step process. Also appears as an example IPsec HMAC algorithm.

nodes.label: Message Authentication Code
nodes.rationale: A keyed integrity check, kept separate from the encryption key because one key should not serve two cryptographic functions. In the chapter's toy TLS, each direction has its own MAC key, and the MAC covers data, record type, and sequence number so reordering and replay of records are detectable. IPsec ESP places a MAC, created with a shared secret, in the ESP authentication field.

nodes.label: Nonce
nodes.rationale: A number used only once so a challenger can check that the peer is live. Returning the nonce under a shared secret or a private key stops a recorded authentication message from being reused. The same idea appears as TLS sequence numbers and nonces, IPsec sequence numbers, and the WPA2 handshake nonces.

nodes.label: Public Key Cryptography
nodes.rationale: Sender and receiver do not share a secret key. A public encryption key is known to all and a private decryption key is known only to the receiver. Cited origins are Diffie-Hellman 1976 and RSA 1978. The chapter also uses it for authentication, digital signatures, integrity, and agreeing a symmetric key.

nodes.label: QUIC
nodes.rationale: The chapter's HTTP view of the stack: HTTP/2 over TCP can sit above TLS, while HTTP/3 is HTTP/2 over QUIC, and QUIC incorporates TLS, over UDP.

nodes.label: RADIUS
nodes.rationale: Example authentication server for enterprise Wi-Fi and for EAP. Holds client credentials and access rights. A local RADIUS server may proxy the decision, as in Eduroam (a visited network asks the user's home realm) or a local directory such as Azure Active Directory.

nodes.label: RSA
nodes.rationale: Rivest, Shamir, and Adelman public-key algorithm. The public key is (n, e) and the private key is (n, d), built from two large primes; encryption and decryption are modular exponentiation. Security rests on the hardness of factoring n. Applying the private key and then the public key also recovers the message, which is what signatures use. Exponentiation is slow, so RSA is used to exchange a symmetric session key rather than to encrypt bulk data. TLS 1.3 no longer offers RSA as a key-exchange choice.

nodes.label: Secure E-mail
nodes.rationale: Confidentiality uses a fresh symmetric key on the message and the recipient's public key on that symmetric key. Integrity and authentication sign the message hash with the sender's private key. Combining all three uses the sender's private key, the recipient's public key, and a new symmetric key. The signed-only form sends the message in the clear.

nodes.label: IPsec Security Association
nodes.rationale: Directional state between a sending and a receiving entity before data is sent. State includes a 32-bit Security Parameter Index, the SA interfaces, the encryption and integrity algorithms, and their keys. Sequence numbers on the SA let the receiver reject duplicate authenticated datagrams using a window rather than a full history. Endpoints store this state in the security association database.

nodes.label: Session Key
nodes.rationale: A fresh symmetric key used for bulk encryption after public-key cryptography has established it. The slides say DES is at least 100 times faster than RSA, so RSA only carries the session key.

nodes.label: SHA-1
nodes.rationale: US standard cited as NIST FIPS PUB 180-1, producing a 160-bit message digest. TLS 1.3's HMAC discussion names SHA-256 and a slide figure '284', which is not this 160-bit SHA-1.

nodes.label: SSL
nodes.rationale: Secure Sockets Layer, the earlier secure-socket design. The slides mark SSL deprecated in 2015, with TLS as the deployed successor. IKE's public-key mode is described as similar to an SSL handshake.

nodes.label: Stateful Packet Filter
nodes.rationale: Tracks TCP connection setup and teardown, and times out inactive connections, so a packet is admitted only when it belongs to a connection the firewall has seen. The access-control list gains a check against that connection table.

nodes.label: Stateless Packet Filter
nodes.rationale: Decides forward or drop per packet from header fields: source and destination IP addresses, TCP/UDP ports, ICMP type, and TCP SYN and ACK bits. Rules sit in an access-control list of (action, condition) pairs applied top to bottom, which the slides compare to OpenFlow forwarding. It does not remember whether a connection exists.

nodes.label: Symmetric Key Cryptography
nodes.rationale: Alice and Bob share one secret key used both to encrypt and to decrypt. The open problem is how they agree on that key if they have never met.

nodes.label: TLS
nodes.rationale: Transport-layer security above TCP, used by nearly all browsers and web servers. Provides confidentiality by symmetric encryption, integrity by cryptographic hashing, and authentication by public-key certificates. TLS 1.3 is RFC 8846 (2018). A toy construction in the chapter separates handshake, key derivation, record transfer, and authenticated close: four keys (encryption and MAC, each direction) come from a key derivation function over a master secret, and each record carries a MAC so integrity is not delayed until the connection ends. A close record type, covered by the MAC, marks a genuine end of data.

nodes.label: TLS 1.3 Cipher Suite
nodes.rationale: The set of algorithms for key generation, encryption, MAC, and digital signature. TLS 1.3 (2018) limits the choice to five suites instead of the 37 in TLS 1.2 (2008), requires Diffie-Hellman rather than DH or RSA, and uses authenticated encryption instead of separate encryption and authentication. Four suites are based on AES. The slide says HMAC uses SHA (256 or 284); 284 is not a standard SHA length and may be a typo for SHA-384. The 1-RTT handshake carries cipher suites, DH parameters, and a server-signed certificate. The 0-RTT resumption encrypts early application data under a resumption master secret from an earlier connection; the slides note it is exposed to replay and discuss it for requests that do not change server state.

nodes.label: 3DES
nodes.rationale: Strengthens DES by encrypting three times with three different keys. Also named later as an example IPsec ESP encryption algorithm (3DES-CBC).

nodes.label: WEP
nodes.rationale: Wired Equivalent Privacy, the earliest named Wi-Fi security mechanism on the chapter's timeline, preceding WPA (2004), WPA2 (2004), and WPA3 (2018).

nodes.label: WPA2
nodes.rationale: Wi-Fi Protected Access generation from 2004. Personal mode (WPA2-PSK) uses one pre-shared password between the device and the access point: open 802.11 association, then an 802.1X four-way EAPOL handshake that uses nonces and a message integrity check to install a one-time AES session key. The shared password is not sent on the air. Enterprise mode uses per-user passwords or certificates, with EAP between the device and an authentication server and the access point mostly relaying.

nodes.label: WPA3
nodes.rationale: 2018 Wi-Fi Protected Access generation. The slides place it with WPA2 in both personal (pre-shared key, device to access point) and enterprise (per-user credentials via an authentication server) deployments, without a separate cryptographic description.

nodes.label: Chapter 8 Network Security
nodes.rationale: Kurose and Ross, Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach, 9th edition (Pearson, 2025), Chapter 8. The chapter moves from security goals and cryptography to secure e-mail, TLS, IPsec, Wi-Fi and 5G, then firewalls and intrusion detection.

nodes.label: Access and Availability
nodes.rationale: Services must remain accessible to legitimate users. The chapter treats denial of service as the threat to this goal and firewalls as one operational control.

nodes.label: Authentication
nodes.rationale: Sender and receiver confirm each other's identity. A name, a source address, or a reusable password is not enough on a network; later protocols add a nonce, a key, and a certified public key.

nodes.label: Confidentiality
nodes.rationale: Only the sender and the intended receiver should understand the message contents. The sender encrypts and the receiver decrypts.

nodes.label: Message Integrity
nodes.rationale: Sender and receiver detect whether a message was altered in transit or afterwards.
